Sports.title: Cherki cracker caps Manchester City win at Liverpool in face of Anfield taunts
Sports.content:
It is a soundtrack that Manchester City have heard before but never for such sustained spells during a match. It came from the Liverpool support, first ringing out around Anfield before kick-off and coming at regular intervals thereafter.

It was always going to be like this as City felt their way into a new reality, one conditioned by the guilty verdicts handed to them by an independent commission on virtually all of the 115 charges they have faced for breaking the Premier League’s financial rules. City maintain their innocence and have appealed.

The Kop wanted to tell City what they are. And where they were going. They wanted to tell them again and again. According to them, they are cheats, who are set to be relegated. It was not exactly a bear pit of an atmosphere; not truly intimidating. It was just an outpouring of anger and it was impossible to ignore.

City did not care. They rolled with the invective. And after a slow-burn contest turned on a second yellow card for the Liverpool midfielder, Ryan Gravenberch, in the 62nd minute, City cut loose. All that their players can do is try to blot out the noise. They did so here, running all over Liverpool’s 10 men to maintain their 100% start to the Premier League season. The key theme from them – and their fans – was defiance. City intend to keep doing what they do.

It was Erling Haaland, inevitably, who lashed them in front and Jérémy Doku, on as a game-changing substitute in the 56th minute, who curled them further ahead with a beauty. The best was still to come. Again, Doku was involved. And after Rayan Cherki dummied a pass from Elliot Anderson, he ran on to a backheel from another substitute, Josko Gvardiol. Cherki had work to do. He did it when he cut away from Jeremie Frimpong, on as a substitute, and rolled home. It was a team goal marked by individual brilliance.

Liverpool were broken and en route to a first defeat under Andoni Iraola. The manager was undermined by the absence of arguably his three best players so far this season; Dominik Szoboszlai, Cody Gakpo and Alexander Isak all picked up injuries during the international window. Liverpool lacked punch.

City had reason to curse the timing of this fixture. Apart from Manchester United at Old Trafford, it could hardly have been worse than a visit here. And not only because Liverpool were one of the clubs most seriously undermined by their accountancy practices. City sneaked their team buses around the back of the stadium on the way in, avoiding the jibes from the streets, but it only postponed the inevitable. It was always going to be lively.

When the Premier League published the document that provided the first raft of detail about the decisions against City on the Tuesday before last, it hit hard. It was the weight of the language – how it dripped with contempt – as well as the sheer extent of the transgressions. Proven misconduct. Sham arrangements. Concerted attempts to frustrate the investigation. How some of the club’s witnesses gave evidence that they knew to be untrue. It served to frame this game. It will continue to frame each one that City play for the foreseeable.

View image in fullscreen Jérémy Doku doubles Manchester City’s lead with a stunning curling shot. Photograph: Michael Regan/Getty Images

The City fans came armed with scores of inflatable bananas. Some of them wore old-school replica shirts. There was a message in there somewhere. Maybe to say that their club predates the Abu Dhabi takeover. It was also possible to spot banners in support of Khaldoon al-Mubarak, the club chair.

You want banners? The Kop had that boxed off. There were some that riffed off Oasis lyrics, including one with the line that “after all, you really robbed us all”. The most eye-catching was unfurled before kick-off, featuring the word ‘cheats’ and a very long sequence of pound signs.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

There was very little to report in terms of first-half action. Even the melee that broke out in the 12th minute after Alexis Mac Allister tussled with Anderson was the definition of handbags. There were no big chances; the precision on the final ball was frequently absent.

Iraola gave Lewis Koumas a full league debut up front and it was the 21-year-old who had the first decent effort straight after the restart. Gianluigi Donnarumma stood tall to save. Liverpool upped the intensity and they had a spell where they pushed and the Kop felt the breakthrough was coming. Gravenberch worked Donnarumma. Mac Allister volleyed wide.

View image in fullscreen Ryan Gravenberch (right) walks off after receiving a red card from the referee Chris Kavanagh. Photograph: Michael Regan/Getty Images

Haaland blew a glorious chance from an Antoine Semenyo pass on the hour, dinking past the far post but City had otherwise created little. Then everything changed. Gravenberch caught the eye with his surging runs but he was on the wrong side when he challenged Doku, who was ready to spark a counterattack. It was clumsy from the Dutchman, the contact on Doku not exactly strong. But having been booked at the start of the second half for a foul on Anderson, Gravenberch was running an almighty risk. He did not get away with it.

City had their opening and how they piled through it. The way that they overwhelmed Liverpool was really something; a demonstration of their strength. It was not a game for the neutral. Are there any such viewers where City are concerned any more? Doku almost teed up Nico O’Reilly and City were on their way when Haaland swept home from a deflected Doku cross. A new reality? It was the same old City on the pitch.

Sports.title: Premier League returns in shadow of Manchester City’s judgment day | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
The Cimbri are heading menacingly south, but in Rome life goes on. The asteroid is definitely coming this way, but people go to work, eat, drink, plan as usual. The White Walkers are approaching the Wall, but the squabbles between the great houses go on. Everyone in the Premier League knows the crisis is approaching, thinks – hopes, fears? – it may be apocalyptic, but until it arrives, what can you do but carry on?

After any break, there’s always an awkward moment while everybody resets. What was the cliffhanger we left the soap opera on? What new plotline had just been seeded? This is one of the reasons international weeks are so disruptive. It’s not just that the Premier League story slows for a while, it’s that we are reminded that these entities are not eternal but alliances of convenience between paid employees who have a life outside the soap opera.

But there has never before been an international break so disruptive as this, never such a sense of unreality about a weekend of Premier League football. It’s not that, the 2022 World Cup aside, this has been the longest international break in history. Nor can anyone, surely, be unaware of the dominant narrative of this window: between 2009 and 2018, Manchester City cheated. Perhaps an away game at Anfield for City is not quite the event it was when Pep Guardiola and Jürgen Klopp were at their peak, but it should still be a great footballing occasion. Yet this was an afternoon when the football felt secondary.

City continue to protest their innocence, clinging to the now-familiar formula that they have a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence that will somehow clear their name, if only people wouldn’t keep refuting it. They have launched an appeal, but if that fails the sanction is likely to be unprecedentedly severe. Do their games matter? Will they be annulled before the season’s end? Was this victory just the difference between finishing the season on -100 points and -97? Could they be expelled from the league? Until sentence is announced, there will an air of provisionality about everything they do. It’s the seconds after an incident that everybody knows VAR will check, the ghost football that might be cancelled, but extended for weeks.

This, though, is not only an issue of the present; it’s an issue of the past. The sanction may or may not strip City of their titles. Many City fans will ignore such a punishment, continue to claim those honours, will point out that memories cannot be so easily extinguished. But even if City’s appeal is successful, or even if the sanction does not relitigate the past, there will be asterisks there in the minds of those who are not City fans, and perhaps also in the minds of some of those who are. Add in Chelsea’s offences, and the Premier League is coming to the end of an 18-year period in which very little was quite as it seemed.

View image in fullscreen Manchester City fans remain defiant despite the guilty verdict against the club they support. Photograph: Michael Regan/Getty Images

The inflatable bananas brandished by City’s support at Anfield on Sunday may have harked back to an earlier, more innocent era, but there is no going back. City are not the club of Imre Varadi any more; as it stands they are the club guilty of the greatest act of cheating in English football history. Their fans can do the Poznan in a spirit of resistance, but they cannot turn their back on the shame their leaders have brought upon them.

What that means for the longer-term credibility of the league can only be guessed at. The basis of sport is faith. Incredible finishes mean little if nothing can be believed. Why go through the emotional agonies if a result might be struck off a decade later for offences committed in the air-conditioned offices of a distant state? Will the City decision undermine faith, or reaffirm it, come as proof that cheats do not prosper, that they will – eventually – be exposed, that the Premier League, almost alone in this grubby world of compromise with and abasement before the mega-rich, is prepared to do what is right?

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

City were booed, there were some chants of “going down” and there were a handful of banners, but Anfield was not the seething pit of disgust many had anticipated. Nor was there much City-related fury at other grounds, although Manchester United fans, erasing all the silverware of the past 15 years, reinstituted their counter on the Stretford End recording the length of time since City last won a trophy. The general sense is of bafflement and bewilderment; what does this mean? What might happen?

It is as though the scale of City’s offences have not yet been fully grasped, that no one quite knows what might happen next. City fans, similarly, seem set on a policy of defiance, as though the scandal is something that has been done to them, rather than the result of the actions of their own directors. To an extent, that is understandable. Until the sanctions are announced, until the result of the appeal is known, the sense of unreality, the phoney war, will go on. The crisis is coming, but its impact has not yet been felt.

Sports.title: ‘We make our own noise’: Maresca hails Manchester City after Liverpool triumph
Sports.content:
Enzo Maresca praised Manchester City for “making their own noise” at Liverpool as they brushed aside the controversy and threats surrounding the club with a comprehensive 3-0 win at Anfield.

City, in their first outing since the club were found guilty on 114 charges relating to Premier League financial rules, maintained their 100% start to the season courtesy of goals from Erling Haaland, the excellent Jérémy Doku and Rayan Cherki. A sixth successive league win ensured Maresca equalled the best start to a managerial reign in Premier League history and kept City at the top of the table.

The City head coach said: “My message to the players since we were together three days ago, when they all came back from their national teams, has been quite clear: guys, the noise will always be there so it’s about how we learn to deal with the noise and it’s our duty to make our noise. Our noise is to win games in the way we did today and to be happy. It was our fans making the noise at the end of the game today.”

Maresca smiled when asked whether he needed City’s appeal to be heard as quickly as possible in order to celebrate such an impressive win. “You cannot imagine how happy I am,” he replied. “I don’t care. I’m here to try and prepare games and to win games. Hopefully I can speak about this situation when we win the appeal.”

City’s chief executive Ferran Soriano was present at Anfield as the fallout from the club’s guilty verdict continues. Maresca reflected: “We were all together. For the importance of the game, Liverpool away, Anfield away, it was a good idea from the club to be all together. That togetherness is what we need.”

The game turned on the 62nd-minute dismissal of Liverpool midfielder Ryan Gravenberch for a second bookable offence. Haaland opened the scoring one minute later and City then ran riot.

Andoni Iraola, the Liverpool head coach, said: “We played two different games: one until the red card, and one from the red card until the end. I think we were the better team until the red card and they were better than us, obviously, after the red card. But I think the players deserve credit today because they’ve given everything.”

Iraola insisted Gravenberch’s red card was harsh. “I think the first foul of Ryan is never a yellow card, never,” he added. “The referee doesn’t even call the foul straight away. He lets it go, Elliot Anderson does a couple of steps and then decides to go down. I don’t know why he shows the yellow card after that because it’s not a situation where it leaves an advantage.”

Sports.title: Impervious City shrug off chaos and controversy to silence Anfield | Andy Hunter
Sports.content:
Anfield welcomed Manchester City to their new reality, a sullied place where every touch is accompanied by cries of “cheat”, any favourable decision is considered proof of further conspiracy and every victory hollow. But Welcome to Hell this was not. The only body of irrefutable evidence in City’s favour since the guilty verdicts landed is that Enzo Maresca’s league leaders appear immune to prosecution and persecution.

That may well change depending on the outcome of City’s appeal and any punishment that eventually arises, likewise the merits and value of a commanding 3-0 win on Liverpool soil. The sight of Erling Haaland savouring a statement victory in front of City’s supporters after the final whistle, while chants of “going down” echoed around the rest of the stadium, captured the schism at the heart of this Premier League season.

City were transformed by the introduction of Jérémy Doku and the dismissal of the Liverpool midfielder Ryan Gravenberch. They were never intimidated, always composed and look a genuine threat to Arsenal’s defence of the title. And yet this could prove their last Premier League appearance at Anfield for the foreseeable future.

It may be difficult, nigh on impossible, to sustain this level of motivation and desire knowing that relegation beckons. Knowing that no one outside City will give them credit for another title triumph did not affect them here, however.

In the 17 days since news of City’s guilt first emerged, and the gestation period of a prolonged international break, their return to action in a Premier League undermined and distorted by their 114 breaches had been built up as a chastening day of reckoning for Maresca’s side. It proved nothing of the sort.

Anfield can still make its voice heard to seismic effect and in the frantic start when Liverpool flew at City, with a fired-up Ronald Araújo whipping up the crowd after winning a challenge against Antoine Semenyo, the collective sense of injustice at a club pipped three times to the title by those in sky blue inspired Andoni Iraola’s players. But bear pits rarely feature in the corporate packaged world of Premier League entertainment 2026.

The “reception committee” for the City team coach before the game was populated by fans carrying selfie-sticks and club shop carrier bags, not an incensed brooding mob. At half-time the Kop was asked to cheer on corporate guests of the club sponsor Standard Chartered as they took part in a penalty shootout, many clearly kicking a ball for the first time in their lives.

There were incessant chants of “you cheating bastards” and various banners of damning judgement, many with an Oasis twist that may have been appreciated by Noel Gallagher in the away end. “And after all you really robbed us all” read one. “All of your stars are fading away,” read another. “A generation of supporters cheated,” cut to the heart of the issue confronting not only Liverpool but the Premier League itself.

View image in fullscreen Liverpool supporters point out that their side finished second to Manchester City three times in the space of eight years. Photograph: Peter Byrne/PA

The City support responded in kind. “In Khaldoon we trust – we’ve won it all!” proclaimed the away flags. The visitors, while performing the Poznan before kick-off, also reclaimed one of the “Cheat” flags that had been doing a healthy trade outside the ground before the game. The inflatable bananas that were once part of the City fanscape also made a comeback, a throwback to more innocent days when their club was not in the dock for inflating sponsorship deals. There was more bickering than tangible animosity. The four men who walked on to the pitch carrying the Premier League hoardings before kick-off received a more hostile reception than City’s players when they appeared for the warm-up.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The decision for City’s team coach to arrive by a different route ensured a tame reception for the visitors. All eyes were on the usual entrance on Anfield Road as City were ushered in from the opposite side of the stadium. It meant even the referees’ chief Howard Webb could walk in almost unnoticed. The hostility cranked up as soon as the contest started and City, using their vast experience to telling effect, gradually drained the venom from the atmosphere and the threat from a depleted Liverpool team. But it was the 62nd-minute dismissal of Gravenberch that had the greater bearing on the outcome.

Doku proved a devastating substitute for Iliman Ndiaye and tormented Liverpool from the left, being involved not only in the red card but all three City goals. The hosts, minus their two most potent attacking players this season in Cody Gakpo and Alexander Isak, plus a hamstrung Dominik Szoboszlai, had no answer with Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola largely anonymous.

The Kop made no calls to be handed the trophies lost to City – and what would that really mean now anyway? – but took solace in demanding that punishment be served in the form of relegation this season. “No trophies for 50 years, que será, será,” the home crowd chanted. But there was no immediate retribution for Liverpool here. City dealt with the chaos and the controversy serenely.

Sports.title: Pino finishes off Nottingham Forest on Glasner’s unhappy Crystal Palace return
Sports.content:
It is fair to say Oliver Glasner has had more enjoyable afternoons. The Nottingham Forest head coach arrived in south London dressed like a bouncer from All Bar One in a black bomber jacket, as if he was anticipating trouble, but was instead given a rapturous reception by the home fans who used to worship him.

The generosity towards their former manager seemed to have extended to Palace’s players as Dan Ndoye was handed a goal in the third minute. Pierre Sage’s side were awful in the opening 40 minutes. Yet Forest could not find a way to beat Walter Benítez again as Liam Delap missed a golden chance to extend their lead and the Argentina goalkeeper’s heroics inspired a thrilling comeback that secured Sage’s first home victory in the Premier League since taking over from Glasner in the summer.

The irony that Daichi Kamada, who won the Europa League under Glasner while they were at Eintracht Frankfurt before he brought him to Selhurst Park on a free transfer, should score his first Premier League goal to equalise in his 68th appearance was surely not lost on the Austrian.

But he and the notoriously trigger-happy Evangelos Marinakis – the Forest owner who was conspicuous by his absence from the directors’ box after his public spats with his Palace counterpart, Steve Parish – will have serious concerns about how his team capitulated after conceding the equaliser. Jefferson Lerma bundled home the second from a corner just before half-time and Yéremy Pino wrapped up the points with a goal that was greeted with a chorus of: “You’re getting sacked in the morning”, directed towards Glasner.

“Call it karma or whatever but it was like I didn’t deserve to win at Selhurst Park because the players did everything,” said Glasner, who claimed not to have heard the taunts from the Palace fans. “I think this was the most dominant Nottingham Forest performance. But not the right result. So, this gives me confidence. My job is not to be influenced negatively by the result.”

There has been plenty of water under the bridge since these two sides met here 14 months ago. Marinakis is suing Palace and “persons unknown” after a banner featuring an incendiary cartoon of him was unfurled during the first half of that game, with the supporters’ group that is thought to have been behind it having since disbanded. Glasner’s decision to join Forest in the summer only added to the ill-feeling that was created by the dispute over Palace’s demotion from the Europa League last season, even if the Austrian was given a warm welcome before and after the game.

The home fans made it clear where their grievances remain as they immediately launched into the anti-Uefa and Marinakis song that was the soundtrack to their Conference League triumph under Glasner, while the Forest supporters responded with taunts of: “We’ve got Ollie Glasner”. They had more reason to celebrate after only two minutes when Anan Khalaili’s weak header presented Ndoye with the chance to run through and score. Forest could barely believe their luck.

View image in fullscreen The Nottingham Forest head coach, Oliver Glasner, responds to a generous reception from the Crystal Palace supporters. Photograph: Andrew Couldridge/Action Images/Reuters

They piled on the pressure, with makeshift defender Lerma – only playing in the absence of the suspended Axel Disasi – looking particularly vulnerable. Jaydee Canvot was guilty of losing possession when Morgan Gibbs-White picked out the unmarked Ndoye and Benítez tipped over before Daniel Muñoz was inches away from scoring against his former club.

But the momentum shifted firmly towards the hosts thanks to a miraculous save from Benítez – deputising for the injured Dean Henderson – that denied Delap from three yards out after Gibbs-White’s shot rebound off the crossbar. “Walter made a save with a lot of bravery,” said Sage, who refused the opportunity to gloat about beating Glasner. “It’s not about revenge,” he insisted.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Delap spurned another golden opportunity with his head and Forest were made to pay just before the break when Kamada scrambled home inside the six-yard area after Jørgen Strand Larsen’s pass deflected straight into his path. Suddenly Palace found their belief. Tyrick Mitchell’s volley was tipped over and from the resulting corner Lerma leapt highest and the ball squirmed through the legs of Matz Sels and just over the line. Replays suggested that Lerma’s effort grazed the arm of team-mate Khalaili on its way in, but VAR let the matter go.

One characteristic Sage has inherited is his team’s difficulty in defending set pieces and Palace were lucky to escape when a header from Gibbs-White at the start of the second half was deflected on to the post by Mitchell. Forest looked at sixes and sevens at the other end when Lerma again caused chaos from a corner but they scrambled the ball away.

There was no such reprieve a few minutes later when Quinten Timber’s pass was diverted into the path of Strand Larsen and Pino made no mistake with the rebound. The Spain forward then turned provider but Strand Larsen could not find a way past Sels. That didn’t stop the Palace fans from gleefully asking Glasner what the score was. Ndoye and Neco Williams had chances to make things interesting late on but Forest – and Glasner – had been humbled by then.

Sports.title: Mohamed Belloumi grabs point for Hull in seesaw draw with Everton
Sports.content:
Hull retained their unbeaten home record since returning to the Premier League with an entertaining draw against Everton at the MKM Stadium.

Brennan Johnson found the net in the 34th minute but was denied a first Premier League goal for Everton following a video assistant referee check, leaving the sides to go in goalless at the break. The hosts wasted little time after the interval, however, as Joe Gelhardt opened the scoring in the 48th minute following an error by Ainsley Maitland-Niles.

Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall equalised for Everton seven minutes later, and Thierno Barry, who had squandered plenty of earlier chances, then put the visitors ahead midway through the second period. Hull responded swiftly, though, with the substitute Mohamed Belloumi pulling the home team level in the 74th minute.

The Tigers have returned to the top flight with an unexpected bang, tasting defeat for the first time in their final fixture before the international break at Newcastle. They were slow off the mark in the early exchanges here, but eventually produced a forward burst of play that saw both Oli McBurnie and then Lewie Coyle threaten before being thwarted.

Gelhardt caused danger with a run down the right in the 22nd minute but his shot was comfortably collected by Jordan Pickford. Matt Crooks got his head to a corner 10 minutes later, but James Tarkowski cleared and play sped to the opposite end.

Barry unleashed a shot that was gathered by Konstantinos Tzolakis, but the ball rolled from his hands and was fired in by Johnson for what appeared to be the opener 11 minutes before half-time. But, after a lengthy VAR check, the winger was ruled offside. Gelhardt and Nobel Mendy then went close to easing the nerves of home fans with near-misses before half-time.

The hosts did not have to wait long for the opener after the break though. Sorba Thomas capitalised on a mistake from Maitland-Niles and fed Gelhardt, who coolly nudged the ball beyond Pickford in the 48th minute.

The Everton response was fairly rapid, however, and Maitland-Niles atoned for his slip-up by finding Dewsbury-Hall, who headed home in the 55th minute.

View image in fullscreen Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall heads home to make it 1-1. Photograph: Lee Parker/CameraSport/Getty Images

Barry, who had much to ponder after missing two earlier chances, then redeemed himself when he pounced to lash beyond Tzolakis to put the visitors ahead for the first time in the match.

But Hull, who had made a handful of changes, were not behind for long as the substitutes Elliot Stroud and Belloumi linked up and the latter sent a left-footed shot past Pickford in the 74th minute to secure a point for the Tigers.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

David Moyes felt his Everton squad completely underperformed. Change is afoot at the club after it was announced earlier in the week they would be put up for sale, but their manager was in no mood for excuses after the draw.

He said: “I’m really disappointed that we didn’t come away with three points, I couldn’t see them getting a goal when we went 2-1 up – I thought if anything we would go on and finish it. It looked really unlike us, the way we gave the goals away today, it was very, very poor.

“Hull have had some great results here, against Manchester United and Villa, they’re not easy to beat and they weren’t [today] but I thought we should have gone on and won the game comfortably.

“The overall performance from everyone was so far below our level, way below where we should be. I’m not giving the players any room for excuses because of what’s going on, whether that be the transfer window or that be ownership.”

Sports.title: European football: Freiburg move top of Bundesliga while Isco keeps Betis flying high
Sports.content:
Ten-man Freiburg scored an 85th-minute winner ⁠through Keisuke Goto to snatch a 2-1 home victory over ⁠Schalke 04 ⁠on ​Sunday and move top of the Bundesliga.

Freiburg, who had ⁠already made a club-record start with 10 points from their opening ⁠four matches, climbed to 13 points, ​ahead of Borussia ‌Dortmund on ‌goal difference. The champions, Bayern Munich, who drew 2-2 ‌against Augsburg on Saturday, are third on 11.

With Freiburg in control, Maximilian Eggestein put the hosts in front after 10 minutes, but Schalke hit ‌back through Adrian Gantenbein on the half-hour. Freiburg were reduced to ​10 men when Yuito Suzuki received a second yellow card in the 64th minute, seemingly handing Schalke the initiative.

But ⁠the visitors were far too passive and ​toothless ​in attack to ​make the extra man count ​and Freiburg ‌punished them ​five ​minutes before the end with the Japan international Goto snatching the winner with a glancing header.

Borussia Mönchengladbach remained rock bottom of the Bundesliga after a 2-1 defeat to local rivals Cologne on Sunday, in a match overshadowed by ugly scenes on the terraces.

The game was suspended for several minutes and riot police surrounded the away block after Gladbach fans appeared to fire fireworks into the home sections after Said El Mala’s superb second-half winner. That maintained pointless Gladbach’s miserable start to the season as the new coach, Alexander Blessin, failed to prevent the club falling to their fifth defeat in as many games.

The Real Betis playmaker Isco scored in each half ⁠as his side breezed to a 5-2 home win over Osasuna on ⁠Sunday that lifts ⁠them ​to third place in La Liga, five points behind the leaders, Barcelona, and one ahead ⁠of Real Madrid.

Isco fired home from the penalty spot in the 10th minute to ⁠open the scoring, and Abde Ezzalzouli added a second ​before the break after ‌Betis won the ‌ball high up the pitch and countered quickly.

Betis ‌looked to be set for a comfortable afternoon when Diego Llorente added a third three minutes after half-time, but two quick goals for the visitors from Ante Budimir and Raúl García reduced the ‌deficit to 3-2 in the 56th minute.

However, Isco eased their nerves again when he ​snapped up a loose ball in the box and rifled it home, and José Antonio Morante came off the bench in the 90th minute before scoring deep ⁠into stoppage time to leave Betis on 19 ​points after ​eight games.

Earlier on ​Sunday, Real Sociedad held off a spirited ​comeback from ‌Deportivo La Coruña ​to ​emerge with a 3-2 win at home, while struggling Elche grabbed a much-needed point by holding visitors Celta Vigo to a scoreless draw.

Lazio moved level on points with Inter at the top of Serie A with a 3-1 win over Monza on Sunday as 10-man Roma played out the first goalless draw of the Italian season at Como.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Nuno Tavares gives Lazio an early lead. Photograph: Riccardo Antimiani/EPA

Under Gennaro Gattuso, who has bounced back after his failure in charge of the Italian national side that missed out on the 2026 World Cup, Lazio continued their strong start to the season. Still unbeaten, the Roman side secured a fifth victory in six matches to pull level on 16 points with Inter, who beat Parma 3-0 at San Siro on Saturday.

Nuno Tavares gave Lazio a third-minute lead and Gustav Isaksen doubled it midway through the first half. Monza had Lorenzo Lucchesi sent off on 35 minutes for hauling down Tijjani Noslin as he broke through on goal, but the 16th-placed visitors rattled Lazio after the break, pulling a goal back and coming close to equalising before conceding a third goal in the closing stages.

Roma left Como frustrated. The dismissal of league top scorer Donyell Malen for a dangerous tackle early in the second half forced them to scale back their ambitions. Neither team could find the breakthrough in a clash between two sides widely regarded as dark horses for the title, leaving Inter and Lazio two points clear of Roma after their respective wins over Parma and Monza.

Bologna picked up their first win of the season by beating Lecce 2-1. Milan remain unbeaten in Serie A after drawing 1-1 with Sassuolo. Adrien Rabiot’s opener was cancelled out by Cas Odenthal as Milan settled for their third draw of the campaign and stay fifth in the table. Juventus are one point behind Milan after an 81st minute equaliser from Randal Kolo Muani salvaged a 1-1 draw with fourth-placed Cagliari.

Marseille put an end to their four-game losing run in Ligue 1 as Amine Harit and Himad Abdelli scored in a 2-0 win at Troyes. Struggling Marseille began the weekend in the relegation zone after suffering five losses in a row in all competitions, but a pair of second-half goals lifted them to 13th place.

Harit steered in a cross from Emerson Palmieri shortly after half-time before Abdelli converted a late penalty as Marseille avoided matching their worst losing streak over the past 40 years. Troyes had gone close to an equaliser just before Abdelli made the points safe for Marseille, but Renaud Ripart’s stoppage-time volley crashed against the post.

Rennes moved up to third earlier in the day with a 4-1 win against Auxerre, while Nice came from behind to beat Strasbourg 2-1.

Sports.title: Scottish Premiership: Celtic end losing skid and take top spot back from Rangers
Sports.content:
Jota made his long-awaited return to action as Celtic claimed a much-needed 2-0 victory at Motherwell to move top of the Premiership again and ease the sense of gloom and tension that had engulfed the club during the international break.

Five months on from a dramatic late win that helped them on their way to last season’s title, Martin O’Neill’s side enjoyed another big result at Fir Park to end a three-game losing streak and climb back ahead of Rangers, who had leapfrogged them at the summit on Saturday.

After a renewal of hostilities between supporters and the Celtic board as well as uncertainty about O’Neill’s future as manager during the three-week break since their home defeat by their bitter rivals, an early strike from Camilo Durán helped restore a semblance of calm for the Hoops.

The champions had control of proceedings thereafter and – despite an inspired display from the home goalkeeper Alex Paulsen – Celtic added to their lead through Benjamin Nygren in the 58th minute as they made it seven wins in eight league matches this term.

The huge Hoops support sporadically unfurled banners and chanted against the club’s major shareholder Dermot Desmond, who was the subject of a tennis-ball protest by a group of balaclava-clad supporters at the Alfred Dunhill Links Championship at St Andrews last weekend. Long before the end of a largely one-sided encounter, however, it was Motherwell’s fans who were displaying their frustration by making for the exits as their insipid side slid to a fourth consecutive defeat.

“If we’d been beaten today, of course, that would have been four on the trot, so that doesn’t help any manager,” said O’Neill. “But we didn’t. For us to get on track again domestically was delightful.”

Derek McInnes praised his Rangers players and blamed the extended international break for some disjointed play in Saturday’s 3-1 win over Kilmarnock.

Rangers went into the break three up at Ibrox after Ryan Naderi twice headed home either side of a Kevin Kelsy strike. But Killie had chances throughout, especially after the interval, before finally getting their reward when the substitute Nicky Clescenco struck on a last-minute counterattack. The visitors ended the game with six efforts on target to Rangers’ four, but the home goalkeeper, Ivor Pandur, was seriously troubled only once before being beaten.

View image in fullscreen Ryan Naderi celebrates after opening the scoring for Rangers against Kilarnock. Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PA

“I was really pleased with how clinical we were in the first half,” said McInnes. “We put the ball in the box, we scored goals. We just didn’t do it enough for whatever reason. But we have to be honest, for long spells we looked like a team that hadn’t been together for the last three weeks. There’s a bit of understanding for me where the players have been. Whoever came up with this idea, it’s such a long time for your players to be away. We pay their wages, we look after our players and for them to be away for nearly three weeks is too long. But we’ve got the job done and credit the players for digging deep and getting three points.”

Hearts eased to their biggest home win in the league for three-and-a-half years as they dismantled St Mirren 5-0 to remain on the coattails of Rangers and Celtic.

Third-placed Hearts dominated from the start and Laurent Mendy fired them ahead in the 20th minute. Calvin Miller scored two penalties, either side of half-time, before goals from Cláudio Braga and Josh McPake ensured a smooth afternoon for Hearts.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Hearts’ Calvin Miller scores his side’s second from the spot against St Mirren. Photograph: Zak Mauger/Getty Images

It was Hearts’ biggest league win at Tynecastle since they defeated Ross County 6-1 under Steven Naismith in April 2023 and they are now comfortably the top scorers in the league. Hearts’ manager, Wouter Vrancken, said: “We try to play a kind of football that is positive and constructive and proactive, and not a reaction. I think people come to the stadium to see nice football, to see goals from your side.”

Josh Fowler’s first-half penalty earned St Johnstone a 1-0 win over Aberdeen putting them into the top five. Fowler’s spot-kick, awarded against Jack Milne after a lengthy video assistant referee check, proved the only goal of the game as the Dons huffed and puffed to no avail in front of goal.

Ashley Hay scrambled in a stoppage-time winner to secure Dundee a 2-1 victory at Falkirk. The striker, out since early August with a ligament sprain, converted from close range after latching on to Ethan Hamilton’s free-kick in the first minute of added time. His goal completed the turnaround after Owen Bevan’s second goal for the Dark Blues had cancelled out Jacob Murrell’s first-half penalty at Falkirk Stadium.

Marink Reedijk endured a disappointing first game as Hibernian’s manager as his side suffered a 1-0 defeat against Dundee United at Tannadice. The hosts scored in the first half through winger Daniel Bennie, on loan from QPR, and the visitors finished the game with 10 men after Jacob Devaney was sent off.

Sports.title: Man City embraced their shame and laughed in the face of English football, no one knows whether their emphatic 3-0 win at Anfield matters. For now cheats do prosper, writes OLIVER HOLT
Sports.content:
Manchester City delighted in a delirious dance with their own notoriety at Anfield on Sunday evening. The team belonging to the club branded the biggest cheats in English sporting history embraced their shame and laughed in the face of the scorn of the rest of football.

On the occasion of their first public outing since they were found guilty by an independent commission of 114 charges of financial chicanery, City defied the revulsion that has been visited upon them and waltzed past Liverpool, the team which suffered most from their cheating, with a comprehensive 3-0 victory. It was another bad day for a game reeling from what City have done to it.

The win restored their three-point lead over Arsenal at the top of the table and extended their record at the start of this season to six successive triumphs but as the football world waits to see whether their appeal succeeds or what their punishment will be, no one knows whether that matters or whether it is utterly meaningless.

The City fans in the away end turned their backs to the pitch in the dying minutes and did the Poznan, the dance of celebration they have made their own. Their celebrations may be muted if, as many expect, they are relegated to League Two at the end of this season.

It is a sign of quite how dysfunctional the Premier League has become that a team with a perfect record, a team that played some wonderful football in the second half, was serenaded with chants of ‘going down, going down, going down’ by the Liverpool fans. They may indeed be going down but they are going to enjoy life while they do.

For them, all the noise was just sound and fury, signifying nothing. For the rest of football, it was a thoroughly dispiriting day. For now, it seems, cheats do prosper.

Erling Haaland celebrates breaking the deadlock at Anfield after Liverpool went a man down

The Reds were beaten 3-0 by City in the visitors' first game since being found guilty

Jeremy Doku netted the second of the game with a brilliant curling effort in front of fans waving inflatable bananas

It will have struck a discordant note for the rest of the game to see them celebrating so wildly at the end when they have been found guilty of serial cheating but the modern City is not a club known for its humility and they are not about to change now. This is a league in limbo but for now, no one can touch them.

The match merely marked the end of an extraordinary day on Merseyside. A couple of hours before kick-off, crowds were already standing five and ten deep on the Anfield Road, as they had done back in the closing weeks of the 2013-14 season when they tried to will Brendan Rodgers and his Liverpool team to the Premier League title with a wall of sound. City won the title that year, of course. It was one of the triumphs that may soon have an asterisk attached to it.

This was a different kind of welcoming party. It was intended to greet the City coach. Some Liverpool fans held up flags bearing the legend: ‘Guilty – 114 Charges’. Beneath the words, there were likenesses of Erling Haaland, Bernardo Silva, Pep Guardiola, Enzo Fernandez and Rayan Cherki dressed as a gang of convicts, looking glum, heads in hands, surrounded by champagne bottles and piles of cash.

Other Liverpool supporters held up flags that simply said: ‘Cheats’, against a sky blue background and the figure ‘114’. Further along the road, red smoke from a flare wafted through the air. The police officers waiting near the Players’ Entrance looked edgy. The temperature began to rise. ‘You cheating bastards,’ the Liverpool supporters yelled in anticipation of the bus arrival, ‘you know what you are.’

It felt like football’s equivalent of waiting to pelt aristocrats with rotten eggs as they rode in tumbrils through the streets. But the City coach did not come this way. It took a back route instead and approached the ground all but unnoticed.

Two buses painted blue and bearing City’s name passed slowly beneath the Sir Kenny Dalglish Stand and, followed by a jogging security contingent, trundled unmolested into an underground car park.

And so on this day, amid subterfuge and shame, City’s new life as the pariahs of the English game began. This is their reality now, after an independent commission decided they were guilty of 114 of the charges of financial chicanery that the Premier League had levelled against them. The rest of English football will treat them as condemned men.

They entered Anfield like fugitives and, as they try to escape the guilt for the financial chicanery that helped them win so many titles between 2009 and 2018 and beyond, fugitives is what they are. It will probably feel that way to the rest of the league until their appeal has been decided and they have faced their punishment. City gave notice on Sunday that, until then, they will laugh in their faces.

City are laughing in the face of football and were delirious in their celebrations

Ryan Gravenberch (right) was sent off by referee Chris Kavanagh in the second half

Anfield displayed banners mocking City after the guilty verdict, including one with 114 pound signs within the word 'cheat'

'A generation of supporters cheated', summed up the sentiment from Liverpool fans

The Anfield crowd left them in no doubt about the extent of the anger that other clubs feel about the unfair advantage they gained for so long. ‘A generation of supporters cheated,’ one banner hanging in the Kop said, articulating the feeling that City stole away the joy of days of triumph from fans of other clubs, days they will never get back.

‘And after all, you robbed us all,’ another banner in the Kop said. At the end of their warm-up, it was that banner in front of which the Liverpool players chose to congregate and salute their supporters. Perhaps it was coincidence. Perhaps it was not. The supporters roared their approval.

'All of your stars are fading away,’ one more sign referencing the work of Manchester band Oasis, said. In the front row of the Kop, home fans unfurled a long, thin, banner that ran for half the length of the stand. It was a row of 114 £ signs, decorated with the word ‘Cheats’.

In many ways, it was sad to see City reduced to this. This is a fine old club brought low by the actions of its owners. Once the standard bearers of the Premier League, once a team that won an unprecedented four top flight titles in succession, City are now a team to be mocked and scorned by supporters of other clubs.

The television cameras picked out City’s embattled chief executive Ferran Soriano sitting in the stands. There was no sign of the chairman, Khaldoon Al Mubarak. That was a surprise on a day when most expected him to make a point of showing solidarity with the club’s players and staff.

It was left – as it is always left – to the most loyal of City’s fans to stand up for the club. What has happened to City is no fault of theirs, of course, and the hard-core travelling contingent – including Noel Gallagher - showed their own defiance in the best way, travelling here to hostile territory and waving an army of inflatable bananas in the air.

Better inflated bananas than inflated commercial income. The yellow fruit was a nod to the times before the Abu Dhabi takeover when City spent time in the lower leagues and their fans did not waver in their support. The bananas were a symbol of that time. For some legacy fans, the prospect of being relegated to League Two holds no fears.

Rayan Cherki scored the third after a great team move as City ran out comfortable winners

Enzo Maresca gestures to the fans after steering his side to victory away at Anfield

City supporters are seen doing the Poznan in a game that ultimately could be meaningless

City fans in the away end celebrated while the rest of football turned away in despair

City’s players, too, were unfazed by their infamy. It was three minutes after half-time when Liverpool conjured the first real chance of the game. The ball fell to Lewis Koumas on the edge of the area and his stinging left-foot shot was beaten away by Gianluigi Donnarumma. Suddenly Liverpool poured forward. Donnarumma saved again from the excellent Ryan Gravenberch. Alexis Mac Allister whistled a shot wide.

But then City took control. Haaland, whose father Alf Inge, was also standing with the City away fans, was played through by Antoine Semenyo but clipped his right-foot shot just wide of the far post.

Many had speculated that at least one of the teams would not finish the game with all ten outfielders on the pitch and they were proved correct three minutes later when Gravenberch was sent off for a second bookable offence, an innocuous push on Jeremy Doku. Fernandez brandished an imaginary card in the referee’s direction as soon as the foul occurred and Chris Kavanagh agreed with him.

Seconds after Gravenberch had trudged off the pitch, City were ahead. Doku cut inside and unleashed a fierce shot that cannoned off Mac Allister. Haaland reacted fastest and lashed an instant drive past Alisson. The goal was scored in front of the away end. The fans there celebrated wildly. The goal must have tasted particularly sweet.

Three minutes later, City were two ahead. Doku teased Victor Munoz on the edge of the Liverpool box, jinked to his right and curled a delicious shot over Alisson. Twelve minutes from time, Cherki completed the victory with the best goal of the lot, running on to an extravagant flick by Josko Gvardiol and slipping the ball beneath Alisson for the third.

The pariahs celebrated in front of their own supporters and punched the air. The rest of football turned away in despair at what the game has become and the uncertainty that stalks it.

Sports.title: Manchester City's first game since guilty verdict: Buses evade baying Anfield mob, AI banners depicting Pep Guardiola in prison clothes but day of fireworks fizzles into damp squib
Sports.content:
The eyes of the world were on Manchester City in anticipation of an Anfield bearpit and a show of visceral hatred after the guilty verdicts handed down by an independent commission.

City's buses have endured serious damage on Merseyside before and they kept their route under wraps, ultimately avoiding any altercations when entering the stadium.

Daily Mail Sport spent the day in Liverpool to observe how hostile the welcome was for a club hated across the country - but nowhere more so than here...

12.39pm

At Lime Street Station, the first few Manchester City supporters are arriving off the train from Oxford Road. A lad wearing a Scream mask mills about. Liverpool city centre is busy but serene, only the stag and hen dos discussing the night before really making much of a scene.

1.34pm

Down Venmore Road, at the back of the Kop, one group of home fans notice their first unofficial merchandise stall. It is draped in the usual half-and-half scarves, but noticeable at a second glance are the more bespoke items available for the occasion. Huge blue flags, depicting Pep Guardiola, Erling Haaland, Phil Foden, Bernardo Silva and Sheikh Mansour in cartoon prison garb, have ‘guilty 114’ plastered on them. Foden’s likeness is up for debate.

Roaring with laughter, a home fan can be heard demanding one for the day. He parts with £15 for the privilege. A cheats flag goes for a tenner. Shirts riffing off the second Oasis album read: ‘What’s the story, trained glory?’

The seller’s patter with his public extends to: ‘Like OJ, it was nailed on, weren’t it?’

Liverpool fans were ready and waiting with AI banners, edited half and half scarfs and t-shirts to humiliate their rivals

Huge blue flags, depicting Pep Guardiola, Erling Haaland, Phil Foden, Bernardo Silva and Sheikh Mansour in cartoon prison garb, have ‘guilty 114’ plastered on them

2.07pm

Anfield Road, the pyro thoroughfare, is beginning to fill up. A police drone buzzes overhead and some of the local constabulary are kitted with gas masks in anticipation of the smoke to follow.

A man there with his daughter is attracting some attention, having decked himself out in the t-shirt and clutching a guilty flag. He loudly pleads ‘no paparazzi’ as he stands in the middle of the street, then shouting that ‘the prisoners are coming’ after noticing some movement further down the road. It feels early and proves a false alarm, ambulances making their way down instead.

Music begins to blare from inside the bar across the way and some begin to clamber up the walls and railings for the main event later.

2.23pm

The chants disparaging Manchester ramp up. And those masks come in handy as red smoke billows. A homemade ‘cheats’ banner – white lettering stitched onto plain red material – is unfurled by a lady on her own, barging to the front of the throng. A City fan wanders around the area without acknowledgement, with police walking up and down the road filming. Security struggle to hold people back in an attempt to keep the road clear.

2.46pm

There is a theory that a string of minibuses are carrying City players. That would certainly dodge any unwanted flashpoints from the visitors’ perspective. With tinted windows, it is almost impossible to peer inside the vehicles but there are seemingly an unusually high amount of them. It could well be that one is carrying City directors Ferran Soriano, Ingo Bank and Hugo Viana.

A fan from the Republic of Ireland says he hasn’t been to a home match for two years but wouldn’t miss this. The atmosphere is lulling to a general murmur.

The Liverpool bus was welcomed by a cloud of red smoke provided by their supporters

The fans were out from early to create a hostile atmosphere around the stadium

2.55pm

Liverpool arrive, quickly motoring into the players’ entrance. The place goes wild. One middle-aged man unveils a ‘Cheating B******* FC’ top complete with City crest and looks immensely proud of his handiwork.

Immediately after, police seem to stop thwarting supporters from walking up and down the road. Are City already inside?

3.09pm

‘F****** s**houses’ comes the disappointing shriek as it becomes clear that the two City buses ferrying the squad and staff inside Anfield have evaded the baying crowd. City’s drivers have gone a different route, going past the Shankly Gates and the away end rather than the more conventional route. They enter via the contractor entrance, about 100 yards from the normal point but those waiting for them do not notice until too late, only chanting once the first is already halfway inside. And are stationed too far away.

3.18pm

Several hundred City fans who came on the coaches park up on Priory Road, which splits Anfield and Goodison Park, and are marched across Stanley Park by police. Much larger drones hover. They sing about cheating when they want, Edin Dzeko and chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak, waving their inflatable bananas. Some posturing with locals ensues, although it is all good natured. Some gawping at the spectacle are wearing fetching friendship scarves down Dahlia Walk behind the away end, only manned by 11 police and two horses. Nine riot buses stand waiting nearby just in case.

The Manchester City buses took a different route to the ground than the usual to avoid the rowdy mob

The home support turned up with shiny balloons mocking the guilty visitors but City's faithful promptly responded with their inflatable bananas

3.52pm

An away supporter is in touch. He says they have received no comments around the train station or pubs. ‘I’ve built this up in my head and it’s been a massive letdown,’ he says. ‘Looks like it’s all about content than real anger. Embarrassing.’

4.22pm

The fan is inside and texting again: ‘This is lame. No difference from any other game I’ve been to here.’

4.27pm

A small banner hanging from the tunnel talks up Steven Gerrard being a Premier League winner in 2014, while City’s contingent enjoy singing about the legend’s infamous slip. Boos as the players emerge, expensive looking 115 balloons are held aloft and Rayan Cherki is jeered at kick-off.

6.27pm

Jubilant City fans are allowed out at the same time as the home supporters and there comes a brief threat of skirmishes outside the away end. Those of a Liverpool persuasion forcefully ask the police why the rivals are not being kept inside to allow crowds to disperse. ‘Yep, we think exactly the same as you do,’ was the reply. Noel Gallagher has left early and Alfie Haaland purposefully strides home through a sea of red shirts. The pantomime is over.

Sports.title: Max Verstappen was brilliant in cruising to Singapore victory... but it's just a matter of time before wonderkid Kimi Antonelli clinches his maiden title, writes JONATHAN McEVOY
Sports.content:
Kimi Antonelli, at 20, is the Formula One champion-elect and nobody can get near to him. It’s all over and the rest can switch their engines off right now.

Yes, Max Verstappen won the Singapore Grand Prix, his 73rd triumph but his first here under the lights of the city track. It was another demonstration of the Dutchman’s brilliance, a dominant win from pole that was never in doubt in a largely boring race.

Antonelli, the great aggregator from Bologna, finished third, separated from Verstappen by Charles Leclerc of Ferrari.

So strong has Antonelli been this season that he can secure the title in Austin, Texas, home of the next race, a week on Sunday. He will do it in the end, wherever he does it, having made practically never a slip even on his average days.

And George Russell, the British drive who carried every hope of accomplishing that dream in the other Mercedes, is gone. Game over. Long blown away. He is 102 points back, and that is nowhere you want to be when your lifetime’s work is on the line.

He finished ninth yesterday. He is resigned to his predicament, though he will not quite so readily admit to it. With six races remaining – if Formula One’s owners follow through on the idea of concluding the season in the Middle East.

Max Verstappen celebrates his second win in a row after a dominant drive

Verstappen successfully handed an early move from Charles Leclerc (right) to stay in front

If they switch to Imola to fill in for the potential absence of one or two rounds in that region of the world after bombs fell on Saudi Arabia yesterday, he remains condemned to disappointment. It’s relevant. This is in brackets, as it were, but he needs to move teams or forever serve as a player in another man’s script – as Antonelli’s Jeeves.

As for Verstappen’s tremendous victory, by 10 seconds over Leclerc, this must be saluted. It reflects the fact that his Red Bull team are on a march and, and that their engine, newly made under the auspices of Christian Horner, who set up the enterprise several years ago before leaving last season, is a huge success.

Lando Norris was fourth and Lewis Hamilton sixth, a place behind Oscar Piastri of McLaren.

Antonelli came up one place from where he started on the grid – he is streets ahead in the overall fight and on the day he did what he needed to do to secure his advantage in this regard. He needs to be 126 points in front after Austin, the next race, to clinch the championship. Nearly a job done at barely out of his teens.

Hamilton was in a war of words with Ferrari as he vied with Leclerc for his track position, deciding to stay out on old tyres, a policy that he later acknowledged did not work, and that he was the one in the wrong.

‘Sorry boys,’ he admitted. ‘I let you down today with that strategy. My call, and I lost us valuable points. I’ll try to make up for it in the next one. A painful lesson, but I take full responsibility for the decisions I made.

Kimi Antonelli, champion elect, added 15 points to his tally and can win the title at the next race

‘Not every call will work out and I can accept getting it wrong but I’m sorry for the team for the points we lost today. They put so much into every weekend and I wanted to deliver more for them. Great job with the pit stop though.’

Hamilton’s Ferrari boss Fred Vasseur said: ‘We asked him to pit. Don’t blame the team guys. Clearly on the radio he apologised and said, “It was my call”. He decided not to stop behind the virtual safety car but we would have been P2 and P3.

‘We were not sure we could go to the end so we chose to stop under VSC. There was a radio message. The driver has apologised that he let the team down.

‘It was very clear. We were P2, P3 on track, we called two of our guys to pit behind the VSC, one of our guys said, “no I prefer to stay on track” or he missed pit entry. Don’t blame the team.’

Lewis Hamilton admitted to a mistake in strategy that cost him a place on the podium

The triumphant Verstappen had no such concerns or recriminations. He said: ‘For sure I can dare to dream (of the title)… but at the same time, I know it is very close, I know it is there – but I need to make sure that I keep doing the best job I can, to go out there and win and perform the best I can.

‘This weekend I don’t feel like I have driven that well. I feel like I could have done a better job.

‘I am looking forward to being back in Austin but, at the end of the day, if I don’t do my job, the result won’t come.’

‘It is very difficult, so it is hard to say if I will be in the fight in Austin. I will just take it race by race and we will see how it goes there.

‘The car has felt a lot nicer from Baku onwards, a lot more balanced. The way that we have turned that around and the progress we have made makes it feel nicer.

‘When you can add podiums and wins too, that’s nice. We are not in the championship fight and that is why I think until the end we will try to have a good time and hopefully add more wins.’

There will be more for him before the end of the year, but the momentum is with Antonelli, drop by drop, increment by increment, and he will be winning the crown - possibly before the month is out.

Sports.title: Xabi Alonso's team-talks are the secret behind Chelsea's rapid starts, says Morgan Rogers - after manager said he had no explanation following two goals in the first three minutes in win over Bournemouth
Sports.content:
By all accounts, Rafa Benitez’s half-time team talk in the 2005 Champions League final was not remarkable. There was no Churchillian speech. He was calm, analytical, and talked tactics, including how Dietmar Hamann was replacing Steve Finnan to switch to three at the back.

However, Benitez added one other instruction before sending his side out of that tunnel in Istanbul, and, according to the man himself, this was the main message. He told them: ‘Try to score early.’

Liverpool’s players listened. They were 3-0 down at the break. By the hour mark, it was 3-3, a six-minute blitz getting them back into the final. As we all know, they then won it via penalties.

Xabi Alonso was in that Liverpool changing room. He scored the equaliser. Now, he is Chelsea’s manager, and the 44-year-old in charge of a side that have turned into kick-off bullies themselves.

They beat Bournemouth 5-1 at Stamford Bridge on Saturday, and were 2-0 up via Jordan Henderson and Morgan Rogers within two-and-a-half minutes. Joao Pedro made it 3-0, just 29 seconds into the start of the second half. So naturally, we asked Alonso what he is telling his team.

Alonso claimed he does not have a clue as to why Chelsea are scoring so early, so often. ‘I have nothing to do with it,’ he said. ‘I have no explanation,’ he added. ‘No credit to me,’ he insisted.

However, Rogers dispensed with that false modesty from his manager when speaking with the media in the mixed zone. Of Chelsea’s six goals scored inside the opening seven minutes of matches this season, this £117million summer signing has accounted for three.

Morgan Rogers celebrates Jordan Henderson's opener after just two minutes against Bournemouth

Rogers had his own theory when asked for one, and said: ‘I put it down to the manager’s team talks. He gets us firing, gets us going. We always want to start off on the front foot.

'It's about starting well and getting the lead. A lot of games, especially at home, we have won after jumping on the back of early goals. It’s a good trait to have which we need to keep going.'

While Benitez was the unemotional type, we are told Alonso is capable of much more animation in the changing room than that which he projects in his press conferences.

Chelsea’s manager has been calling on his players to start their games with ‘good energy’, and he is said to have used this intriguing early scoring trend to his advantage of late in his speeches.

He has reminded his side of their record for ruffling opponents from the get-go and that they have an extraordinary attack which should spread confidence throughout the entire team.

He encourages them to push up the pitch from the first kick, and Chelsea’s supporters know now they cannot be tardy, lest they want to miss their side scoring a goal, or two in Saturday’s case.

Ironically, there is one Premier League fixture in which Chelsea tried the kick-off gimmick of booting the ball straight out for a throw-in to box the opposition inside their own defensive third, and that was in their 3-0 loss at Brentford before the international break. That was the only outing in which they have not scored inside the opening seven minutes.

Rogers doubled the lead in the third minute as Chelsea made a lightning start

Yet Chelsea brought back their speedy start for Bournemouth. There was already additional belief within the changing room. Against Fulham, they led after 38 seconds. Against Brighton: three minutes and 39 seconds. Against Arsenal: 77 seconds. Against Hull: six minutes and 15 seconds.

So even if it did not happen away at Brentford, when they went into this home game with Bournemouth, there was said to be excitement within the group, almost at who will get the first goal this time. It went to Jordan Henderson after 66 seconds, set up by Cole Palmer. Then followed Rogers with their second after 149, assisted by Henderson.

While there are still some concerns surrounding overall control, Chelsea have been helping themselves by starting games with a goal advantage. While Bournemouth were threatening, they saw this lead through, capping it with Henderson’s 25-yard free-kick.

It will be intriguing the next time Chelsea win a foul close to the opposition’s box. While Rogers was away with England, his team-mates practised them by order of set-piece coach Austin MacPhee, and Henderson was scoring more than Palmer. Hence why the 36-year-old won the right to take this one for 5-1.

Henderson even revealed how Palmer said to him as they were positioning the ball: ‘Which corner are we celebrating in when you score?’ In front of goal, the Chelsea confidence is clearly high.

Rogers added: ‘It was worked on this week before I was here. They did it behind my back and then when I got back, I'm off free-kicks all of a sudden, which I wasn't best happy about! But as long as we score, that’s the most important thing.’

Rogers was certainly happy to celebrate Henderson scoring and not only this goal but his first, as Chelsea yet again led mere moments after kicking off.

Sports.title: Andy Burnham vows to publish details of Man City dealings: Prime Minister will 'put out there' material from time as mayor after backlash for comments in support of shamed owners
Sports.content:
Andy Burnham has pledged to publish details of his dealings with Manchester City’s owners following criticism over his support for the club in the wake of its £830million ‘sham’ contracts storm. The Prime Minister said he would ‘put out there’ all of his interactions with the club’s Abu Dhabi-backed ownership after Tory leader Kemi Badenoch demanded he release ‘everything’ connected to his work with City. The row erupted after former Greater Manchester Mayor Mr Burnham reacted to an independent inquiry finding City guilty of 114 charges of breaching Premier League financial regulations between 2009 and 2018. It is alleged ‘sham’ contracts with commercial partners secretly funded £830million for football operations. The club has maintained their innocence and is appealing the verdict. Mr Burnham initially told the BBC he would be ‘really concerned’ if the club’s owners decided to sell City because of the controversy, describing it as ‘a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester’. His comment prompted questions about his relationship with the club’s ownership and led Downing Street to distance itself from the remark. Prime minister Andy Burnham (with Man City chairman Khaldoon Al-Mubarak in 2019) says he will release the details of his dealings with Manchester City in his previous mayoral role No 10 stressed that any wrongdoing established through the process should have consequences. Speaking on The Rest is Politics podcast, Mr Burnham said the football case should be separate from investment the owners had brought to the region. He said: ‘I will quite clearly put out there everything that I have done working with them in my previous role as Mayor of Greater Manchester. ‘None of it is recent, in terms of meetings I had. I only had one significant meeting and that was in 2021. That is right and I will put that all out there. ‘But the football issues, they are serious and have to be dealt with and the process is independent and it has to run its course. But I think everybody should separate the investment issues because they’re not the same thing.’ His intervention comes as scrutiny grows over the relationship between political figures and major investors linked to Premier League clubs. The Premier League said an independent commission found City arranged 'sham' commercial deals with a number of its sponsors during the period, which were part of a disguised funding scheme, whereby those companies were required to pay only a portion of the relevant sponsorship fees. The commission found that the remainder was funded by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan's Abu Dhabi United Group Investment & Development Ltd, which majority-owned the club.

Your browser does not support iframes.

Burnham received backlash for his comments that many felt were 'tone deaf' Shadow sports minister Louie French called for Burnham to also 'come clean' about any meetings since becoming Prime Minister and urged Sport Secretary Lisa Nandy to respond to questions. Man City, now Premier League pariahs, returned to the pitch on Sunday afternoon, beating Liverpool 3-0 at Anfield. The delight of the travelling supporters and players showcased a club embracing their shame and while severe punishments will follow if their appeal fails, for now the club are allowed to continue as usual. Having been found guilty on almost all charges in the biggest cheating scandal in British sporting history, the case has major ramifications at every level of society, including Downing Street. The Premier League is currently in limbo, with City top of the table but seemingly likely to be cast out if the original verdict is upheld. No doubt the content of Burnham's meetings will be eagerly awaited by those following the case and diplomatic tension between Britain and Abu Dhabi is understood to have risen over the case that rocked football.

Sports.title: Gary Neville claims the wait for sanctions against Man City is 'really bad for the Premier League' as Piers Morgan labels it a 'total farce' after Enzo Maresca's side extend lead at top
Sports.content:
Gary Neville claims the wait for sanctions against Man City is 'really bad for the Premier League' as Piers Morgan labels it a 'total farce' after Enzo Maresca's side extend lead at top

Gary Neville has claimed the uncertainty surrounding Manchester City's status is 'really bad for the Premier League' after their 3-0 victory over Liverpool at Anfield.

Enzo Maresca's side played for the first time since the club were found guilty of breaching Premier League financial regulations between 2009 and 2018.

The club maintained their innocence and appealed against the verdict.

If City lose their appeal, the Premier League have a range of sanctions at their disposal – including relegation or expulsion.

Despite receiving a hostile welcome to Anfield on Sunday, Man City earned a 3-0 victory over Liverpool to continue their perfect start to the Premier League season with Maresca's side now three points clear after six straight wins.

Neville, who served as a co-commentator on the match for Sky Sports, claimed post-match that the fixture had underlined to him that the continuing uncertainty is 'really bad for the Premier League'.

Manchester City beat Liverpool 3-0 in their first match since being found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules

Gary Neville claimed the wait for sanctions against Man City is 'really bad for the Premier League' after watching the club move three points clear at the top of the table

Neville cited the use of 'sham' in the independent commission verdict, which was repeatedly used to describe contracts used to help disguise secret funding of more than £830million, claiming people could begin to use the word when discussing the league with City's status unclear.

'A win at Anfield is really difficult, and we should be eulogising them, but there is that thing in the back of your mind,' Neville said.

'At the end of the game it's quite hard because you're imagining that if these guilty verdicts are confirmed that Manchester City are not going to be in the position that they're in, and there's going to be a huge cloud hanging over the whole league.

'This is not good for the Premier League right now, that's what I've just recognised today.

'This is really bad for the Premier League and it's going to continue for a few months.

'The word "sham" was used quite a lot and people will think for the next few months it's a sham league.

'We've heard the word 'cheats' ring round the ground for the last ten minutes of the match. We've heard Liverpool fans singing 'going down' at a team at the very top of the league. You can't get that negativity out of your head.

'What we can do is admire the football, admire Erling Haaland and [Jeremy] Doku and the finishes we've seen, and the [Rayan] Cherki goal.

Enzo Maresca and Man City players celebrated wildly in front of their fans at full time

Piers Morgan claimed Man City winning the title 'could ruin the Premier League' as he called for a punishment to be announced

'The Man City fans can celebrate behind the goal, but the rest of us are wondering what's going to happen and it's damaging right now.'

Man City eased to victory in the second half at Anfield after Ryan Gravenberch was sent off for two bookable offences.

Haaland and Doku struck in a three-minute spell to put Man City 2-0 up, before Cherki sealed victory with the visitors' third of the match.

Man City players and Maresca celebrated in front of their supporters following the triumph, with the head coach later praising his side for how they handled the 'noise' around the match.

Neville's fellow pundit Jamie Carragher claimed there is 'no way' Man City could be allowed to win the league this season if the verdict remains, and stressed the need for a final outcome before the end of the campaign.

'Man City right now are the best team in the league, they are top of the league, but there is no way Man City can be allowed to win the league this year if they are found guilty,' Carragher said.

'That cannot happen.

'We keep using the word sham, the Premier League used the word sham about the last eight years, but we didn’t know it at the time.

'We know it now, we are watching it. That today, what does it mean going forwards. This has to be done before the end of the season, there is no way this can carry on until the end of the season.'

Broadcaster Piers Morgan, responding to Man City's celebrations, claimed the club leading the Premier League was a 'total farce' and called for their punishment to be announced.

'Sorry, but this is a total farce. Manchester City players, and fans, celebrating wildly like nothing has happened - despite the club being exposed as the worst cheats in football history,' Morgan wrote.

'What happens if they win the title again this season? That could ruin the Premier League.'

'The Premier League has to act asap and announce City’s punishment. This cannot go on.'

Kim Kardashian didn't want to be in F1 fans' bad books again as she attended the Singapore Grand Prix on Sunday.

The reality star made sure to patch things up with Sky Sports icon Martin Brundle as she finally spoke to the presenter during his famous grid walk and asked him 'did we get off on the wrong foot?'

She previously 'rudely' ignored the broadcaster in Monaco during a toe-curling encounter which saw her ridiculed by fans on social media.

But it has now been revealed that Kim had her team contact Sky Sports ahead of the race at the Marina Bay Circuit to make sure she wasn't embarrassed again.

The Skims mogul is said to want to make a 'good impression' with F1 fans and in the paddock as her relationship with Ferrari driver Lewis Hamilton continues to go from strength to strength.

An insider exclusively told the Daily Mail: 'Kim's team reached out to Sky Sports to make sure she could do the Martin Brundle grid walk chat due to the backlash she had received last time.
