"I think loyalty matters, especially for an incumbent," Halvorson said. "I think that polished candidates are not a necessary requirement for Longview and Cowlitz County. I think you just have to be authentic."

When a candidate can't rely on the partisan label next to their name on the ballot, they have to lean on other strengths. Halvorson stressed the need to understand local issues.

Longview used to be solely known for the timber industry. It was founded to house employees of the local timber mill. But as the natural resource economy changed and the logging industry shrank, mills closed and jobs vanished.

toggle caption i Jenny Kane/AP

"I do feel like the tariffs have hit a lot of our industry here hard on the federal level," said Halvorson.

That's where John Braun feels he has a distinct advantage in this race. He owns Braun Northwest Inc., an emergency vehicle manufacturing facility. Walking through his manufacturing facility, Braun pointed out all the different materials used to build an ambulance or fire truck. The cost of those materials has increased because of tariffs and the price hike is passed onto consumers, which in Braun's case, mostly consists of American cities and municipalities.

Sponsor Message

Braun thinks that makes him uniquely qualified to advocate for the trades and did so regularly during his time in the state legislature. While Braun has Trump's endorsement, he hasn't pegged himself as a loyalist. One issue he would break with Trump on, Braun said, is tariffs.

"There are some appropriate uses for tariffs. But kind of the indiscriminate use, the broad use, the blanketed use, just that doesn't work," he said. "We need to be a little more thoughtful on tariff policy."

Gluesenkamp Perez backlash

Vancouver, Wash., is the urban center of this congressional district and the city has recently come into its own.

Considered to be part of the Portland, Ore., metro area, many Vancouverites argue their city's identity is unique. Gretchen Hoyt's family has lived here for four generations. She was always slightly resentful of outsiders (and insiders) smooshing the two towns into one.

Vancouver has put a lot of money into development. They have repurposed historic buildings into multiuse spaces and made the downtown more walkable. The city built a waterfront along the Columbia River that houses luxury apartments and classy eateries – the kind of restaurants Hoyt notes are "special occasion meals" because they're too pricey for the locals to eat at frequently.

She admits all the updates have beautified her hometown and inspired residents to spend more of their time and money in Vancouver. The investment has also led to growth and Hoyt worries a place that used to be a reprieve from high Portland housing prices has developed a similar reputation for being unaffordable.

"It's so hard to buy a house here right now," she said. "It's like everything .. is over $700,000 and for things that are just aren't worth that."

Another thing that has changed about Vancouver is its politics.

toggle caption i Amanda Loman/AP

Clark County, where Vancouver is located, has slowly gotten bluer since 2008. Vancouver itself, Hoyt observed, has shifted toward the progressive side of the scale. That progressive tilt proposes trouble for Gluesenkamp Perez, especially since Clark County is one of two counties she consistently won since her first run for Congress.

Sponsor Message

Two congressional votes that have ruffled feathers among Clark County Democrats. Gluesenkamp Perez voted in favor of a Republican sponsored bill dubbed "The Don't Say Trans Bill," which would require parental consent if a public school student wanted to go by a different name or gender in the classroom.

She also voted for the SAVE Act, claiming the controversial Republican-led voter I.D. legislation spawned by Trump would help secure America's election system.

"People feel betrayed because people thought, 'OK cool. She owns her own business. … Really. Like I'm one of you.' Then it felt like that was just a schtick in order to get the blue vote," Hoyt explained.

Gluesenkamp Perez defended her approval of the legislation.

"I do not support noncitizens voting in American elections — and that's common sense to folks in Southwest Washington. Voting in our nation's elections is a sacred right belonging only to American citizens, and my vote for the SAVE Act reflects that principle," she wrote in an April statement.

Gluesenkamp Perez did not respond to NPR's multiple interview requests.

In retaliation for those votes, progressive Democrats in Vancouver put up a primary challenger on Gluesenkamp Perez's left. While the congresswoman ultimately won one of the top two general election seats in Washington's open primary system, it exposed her vulnerability among the district's Democratic base.

"Nobody is happy with Marie, but they're not voting for John. So they're voting their conscience. It feels like the lesser of two evils," Hoyt said.

Beyond the cities

The impact of tariffs, regulation — and the national economy as a whole –- has the ability to make or break rural communities across the district. Any changes are acutely felt in the coastal region.

Kathleen Nisbet, owner of Goose Point Oysters, took over her family's shellfish farm in Bay Center, Wash., a small town of about 200 people next to the Pacific Ocean.

Sponsor Message

Nisbet has lived in the remote Pacific County town pretty much her whole life. She has seen a once prosperous area, which was propped up by aquaculture industries, transition into somewhat of a ghost town.

To her, the vacated businesses are a testament to how regulations have suffocated small shellfish farms. Nisbet counted on her fingers ten different regulatory agencies she must pay and answer to in order to keep her doors open and estimated she spends around $200,000 a year on agency fees.

"The regulations that we have been dealing with for the last 25 years have impacted our areas in that we've lost our farmers and we've lost our fishermen," Nisbet said.

Nisbet isn't against regulation. Her qualms are they aren't streamlined, they change frequently and are cost prohibitive for small and medium sized producers.

Now, Nisbet is dealing with another problem: Trump's trade war.

"We've lost over 50% of our international sales due to the current political climate between us and Asian countries," she said.

The concern is, if the trade wars continue or worsen, that there will be an even steeper decline to the industry area was built on. More farms will close or consolidate with big fisheries. The identity of the area could disappear.

"We need to make sure that we are building community resilience through natural resources, which has been the traditional backbone of our communities," she emphasized.

Nearby Ilwaco has also been on the receiving end of the industrial downfall. While there is some semblance of natural resource extraction, such as timber, seafood catches and cranberries, for the most part, the coastal town of about 1,400 people has had to pivot to invigorate the economy.

The number one industry in Ilwaco is now hospitality. Restaurants, motels and small shops welcome visitors to the town, a significant portion of whom travel through on their way to or from Cape Disappointment State Park. The town has been working to open more businesses that would attract visitors. Most recently, Ilwaco Cider Company, the town's only brewery, opened its doors.

Sponsor Message

Ilwaco councilman Matt Lessnau, who grew up in the town and moved back during the pandemic, said the cidery is the perfect example of what Ilwaco is trying to build.

"It really has been a tremendous asset in really growing the kind of businesses that we want to see grow in Ilwaco," he said.

But there is a limited tourism season. The town makes the majority of its revenue during the summer months and it relies on federal dollars to help with infrastructure needs because the local tax base isn't there — only about half the population lives in the town full time.

The rural parts of Washington's 3rd District may have fewer people but it's still influential. Pacific County voted for Trump in 2024 but also elected Gluesenkamp Perez. She narrowly won this county in 2022, too.

Lessnau said a congressional candidate needs to understand the local issues of the rural coastal towns to be electable. Additionally, he added, the candidate needs to be relatable.

"We have historically valued representatives that understand our economy and our struggles," Lessnau said. "We have a very low tolerance for bulls***."

World.title: Cleveland-Cliffs CEO says he's prepared to fight Canada in court over Stelco layoffs
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The CEO of the American company that owns Hamilton-based steelmaker Stelco says he's prepared to fight the Canadian government in court to preserve Stelco's plan to lay off hundreds of workers.

Speaking Sunday on CBC's Rosemary Barton Live, Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves disputed the government's characterization that the company is violating binding employment commitments under the Investment Canada Act.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said last week that Cleveland-Cliffs' 2024 purchase of Stelco included "undertakings to continue to employ at least the same number of unionized employees and the vast majority of non-unionized employees as were employed when the transaction was announced" through 2029.

"There is no provision in the contract that I have to keep employment at a certain level every single day of the five years," Goncalves said on Sunday. "If that was an imposition of the Canadian government, I would not have accepted."

Goncalves reiterated Stelco's position that the layoffs are a temporary measure until Canada and the U.S. reach a trade agreement, and that the jobs will be restored.

He also said he's open to selling the company and voiced support for U.S. tariffs on Canadian steel, despite Stelco citing tariffs as a key reason for its economic struggles.

WATCH | Goncalves says he's open to selling Stelco: Stelco owner open to selling company amid fight with Ottawa over layoffs | Duration closed caption 10:00 Lourenco Goncalves, CEO of Stelco parent company Cleveland-Cliffs, speaks with CBC's Rosemary Barton following his company's official response to the federal government's threat of legal action amid layoffs at the company’s Hamilton, Ont.-based steel plant. In a letter obtained by CBC News, Stelco says it is not violating employment commitments.

Ultimatum from Canadian government

Joly issued an ultimatum to the company last week: share a plan to save the up to 500 jobs that could be impacted at the Hamilton plant or face potential legal action.

Prime Minister Mark Carney also said last week that Ottawa will "use all powers that we have" against Cleveland-Cliffs as it pursues the Ohio-based company to the "fullest extent of the law."

Stelco Inc. said in a letter responding to Joly that the company will proceed with the layoffs and the government's characterization of the move as a breach of undertakings is "false."

T he company emphasized "Stelco's situation is a result of factors beyond its control," citing the impact of U.S. President Donald Trump's 50 per cent tariffs.

But Goncalves said Sunday he supports steel tariffs against Canada.

"I am in favour of tariffs against all the countries in the entire world that dump steel into the United States," he said, adding that the Section 232 tariffs have brought "the American steel industry back."

A drone photograph shows the Stelco Hamilton Works steel mill, owned by Cleveland-Cliffs, in Hamilton last month. (Carlos Osorio/Reuters)

"I'm in favour of Section 232. There's no doubt about it."

Asked whether he would consider selling the company, Goncalves said, "For a good offer, yes," but added that he still believes the company can "continue to be a good citizen in Canada."

He told CBC News in a previous interview that he "would not have acquired the Stelco if I knew that Canada and the United States would become what they became — enemies in trade."

Layoffs underway

Jordan Williams, a Stelco employee who received a layoff notice last week, is calling on Goncalves to provide a written response to workers' concerns, including a "credible" plan for Hamilton's cold-rolled and coated steel operations in the future.

"What steps will you take to protect jobs, support our families and provide a path back to work?" he said in a statement sent to CBC News Sunday. "These layoffs reach beyond the plant gates and into the businesses and neighbourhoods that depend on Hamilton industry."

Ron Wells, president of the United Steelworkers Local 1005, which covers Stelco workers in Hamilton, told CBC News last week that layoffs are underway and expected to roll out over three weeks.

He said he expects 300 to 350 layoffs in Hamilton, with more at Stelco's Lake Erie Works in Nanticoke, Ont.

Wells told CBC News at the time that Goncalves, who has previously expressed support for Trump and his tariffs, is eager to make it appear as though Trump's tariffs are working ahead of midterm elections in the U.S.

"I hope, basically, the federal government makes an example out of them," Wells said. "We just want to make sure they … follow through with it."

World.title: Trump announces Russia-Ukraine 'energy ceasefire,' which Zelenskyy says he hasn't seen but supports
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he has discussed the possibility of an energy ceasefire with Russia with Prime Minister Mark Carney, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte but is waiting for more information from the United States.

U.S. President Donald Trump had said in a social media post on Sunday that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to what he described as an "energy ceasefire" without offering specifics on terms.

In an interview with Axios, Zelenskyy said Trump's post was the first he had heard of the deal, though a senior Ukrainian official told Reuters that Ukraine was ready to agree to such a ceasefire if Russia was.

In a social media post of his own, the Ukrainian president said he had just spoken with Carney, Stubb and Rutte to discuss the alleged ceasefire announced by Trump.

"Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it is important that Russia support it as well. We are awaiting details from the American side," Zelenskyy wrote on X on Sunday afternoon. "For our part, Ukraine always FULLY supports steps toward de-escalation, the protection of lives, and the decisions needed to end the war and guarantee lasting peace."

The Prime Minister's Office said Carney spoke with Trump on Sunday and that he told the U.S. president that Ottawa has "strong support" for the energy ceasefire.

"The new energy ceasefire being brokered by President Trump between Russia and Ukraine has the potential to significantly de-escalate the war and protect thousands of civilians from harm and hardship," Carney later said on social media.

"Canada calls on Russia to uphold this agreement as we keep working with our Allies to secure a just and lasting peace for Ukraine and Europe."

The announcement comes a day after Trump blamed Zelenskyy for attacking diesel facilities in Russia and contributing to a global shortage. Russia and Ukraine have repeatedly attacked each other's energy infrastructure during the war.

Trump's brief post said only that the ceasefire takes effect immediately and that both sides had agreed to it. "Do not break it!" he said in his social media post.

The White House did not immediately clarify the president's post or add detail. The Kremlin did not provide comment.

Zelenskyy meets with U.S. President Donald Trump during the United Nations General Assembly, in New York on Sept. 22. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/The Associated Press)

Trump, whose war in Iran has been blamed for high diesel prices that are weighing on Republicans' prospects in next month's midterm elections, had previously announced an energy ceasefire in Ukraine in mid-September, though neither side ever confirmed such an agreement was reached.

"Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" Trump wrote on Truth Social.

Earlier on Sunday, Zelenskyy had repeated Ukraine's long-standing position that it was willing to halt attacks on Russian refineries but only if Moscow ceased its own strikes on Ukrainian power infrastructure.

Any such deal would need to come with "real guarantees," Zelenskyy said.

"The real cause of the war in Europe is Russia and Russia alone," Zelenskyy said. "It's possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but Putin does not want to do so."

Promise of elections

In a dramatic deterioration in their relations, Trump on Saturday had warned Zelenskyy that he had "better damn well stop" attacking Russian refineries, and he urged Ukrainians to replace Zelenskyy as their leader via new elections because he had missed several opportunities to strike a deal with Moscow.

Appearing on ABC's This Week on Sunday, Zelenskyy responded that he would organize elections in Ukraine if Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed to a 60-day ceasefire.

Zelenskyy said it was "up to Ukrainians" to choose their leader but noted that there needed to be an end to the fighting first. Ukrainian law prohibits elections under martial law for security reasons.

"Please tell Putin, give us two months, 60 days of total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organize elections," Zelenskyy said.

The Ukrainian leader rejected being blamed for energy price rises, adding that "everybody in the world" knew that the war in the Middle East was a bigger factor.

The steep rise in global diesel prices, which followed the outbreak of the Iran war in February, has become a political liability for Trump's Republican Party ahead of the midterms, when opposition Democrats could gain control of one or both houses of Congress.

On Saturday, Zelenskyy had responded angrily to Trump's announcement of a diesel supply deal with Russia, saying it would embolden Moscow's attacks on Ukraine and lead to a greater loss of civilian lives.

WATCH | Trump brokers deal to buy Russian diesel: Trump reverses course on Russian oil sanctions | Duration closed caption 2:08 U.S. President Donald Trump has announced a deal to import Russian diesel as fuel prices soar, reversing course on sanctions against Moscow. Ukraine is condemning the move, warning it will directly benefit Russian President Vladimir Putin.

In a readout from the PMO on Sunday, Carney told Zelenskyy that Canada believes the Trump-proposed diesel deal with Russia is "in direct opposition" to the goal of supporting Ukraine and that such a move would enrich the Kremlin and help finance its war effort.

Analysts said Trump's diesel supply agreement with Moscow was unlikely to lead to sustained lower fuel prices as the volumes involved were too small.

The diesel deal was also criticized by U.S. lawmakers, including one of Trump's fellow Republicans, Rep. Don Bacon, who said it was time to apply more sanctions, not lift them.

Kyiv residents angry

On the streets of Kyiv, several residents expressed anger at Trump's suggestion that Ukraine should find a new leader willing to make a deal with Putin.

"No one has the right to tell us what to do, especially since elections cannot be held during wartime," said Sabina, a 40-year-old primary school teacher. "In my view, it is a betrayal by our partners," she said, describing Trump's remarks.

Zelenskyy said he would continue discussions with European leaders on Sunday, and there were daily conversations around additional air defence packages, including ammunition for combat aircraft that are used to down Russia's jet-powered drones.

On Monday, Ukrainian Foreign Affairs Minister Andrii Sybiha is due to participate in a European Union foreign affairs council meeting that is expected to discuss increasing sanctions pressure on Russia and advancing negotiations on Ukraine’s EU accession.

World.title: Turkey gravy brand sold in Canada recalled due to undeclared mustard
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A brand of turkey gravy sold in Canada has been recalled because it contains undeclared mustard.

Kevin's Natural Foods turkey gravy is sold in British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba.

The Canadian Food Inspection Agency says the product contains mustard, which is not included on its label.

The agency says the recall was triggered by the company and there have been no reported reactions associated with the product.

It says the turkey gravy should not be consumed by anyone who is allergic or sensitive to mustard and is advising customers not to distribute or sell it.

The agency is investigating and says it is verifying that the product is being removed from the marketplace.

Health Canada recognizes mustard as a common food allergen.

World.title: Disappointed, angry, excited: Albertans weigh in on looming referendum
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Jim Fedor booked Oct. 19 off work to make sure he can vote in Alberta’s referendum.

“I'm looking forward to it. Never voted in a referendum like this before, so it'll be something new,” said Fedor, who stopped at the CBC News pop-up at the Seton library branch in southeast Calgary last week.

“I'm gonna vote Option 1 on the separation question, for Alberta to stay in Canada, and the other nine questions I plan to vote no for each one,” he said. “I'll get there early, and I'm willing to wait to get in and vote.”

“I think it's important for everyone to have their voices heard. A lot of places in the world don't allow voting on much of anything. So I feel quite lucky to be able to vote and make my vote count.”

CBC News set up at the library to get a sense of how Albertans are feeling as the referendum campaigns head into their final week. We set out Post-It notes and markers, and invited patrons to share their thoughts on the question: What are you thinking about as you get ready to vote?

Library patrons left their thoughts at a CBC News pop-up in the Calgary Public Library's Seton branch. (Elise Stolte/CBC)

Parents came by with their kids; high school students stopped in after their classes ended; seniors swung by to pick up books on hold. A low hum filled the busy building.

Some Albertans frustrated at the vote

A few people were excited to vote, like Fedor. Others were just starting to follow the process and had not yet decided how they would cast their ballots; several expressed frustration at even having the vote.

That’s how Christine Nelson was feeling.

“I'm really disappointed. The majority of people do not want to separate, and we have to spend taxpayers’ money to vote on something that's not going to go through unless there's some kind of, you know, crookedness going on. It's ridiculous,” said Nelson.

Charmaine Coutinho, who stopped by with her young daughter, had a similar sentiment.

“I am feeling anger about the increase in racism and otherness caused by legitimizing these extreme perspectives through government actions,” she said. “I am saying no to everything, and we are, and I am, very much in favour of staying in Canada.”

From left to right, Michael Chudleigh, Charmaine Coutinho and her daughter, and Christine Nelson. They all stopped by to share their thoughts at the CBC News pop-up in Seton on Thursday. (Elise Stolte/CBC)

Michael Chudleigh said he is voting the same, but trying to stay open to difference.

“I'm trying not to be angry about the whole thing and understand that those who disagree with me have their reasons, even if I can't see them.”

Friends at odds over separation

One pair of seniors were laughing and chatting as they stopped by on their way for coffee. The two women said they are good friends, who meet regularly.

One is passionate about staying in Canada, while the other is casting her vote to explore leaving.

They don’t talk about the referendum. “We might not be friends after!” said the pro-unity friend. She didn’t want to be interviewed, but earlier said her father fought for Canada and she’d never want to see it splintered.

The other friend came back later to write her thoughts on the whiteboard: “I think the Oct. 19 [referendum] is more like a memorandum of understanding thing and gets people talking and looking into our rights and fairness/democracy. But many people have been led to be afraid it’s a final say or referendum to leave their country or be taken over by Trump!”

She wrote that separatists fear the way Ottawa has been asserting control over individuals, such as freezing bank accounts during the trucker convoy.

Newcomers express love for Canada

As the afternoon wore on, our board filled with messages, with a lot of love for Canada.

“I love Canada; I’ll vote to stay here,” wrote one person.

“I love Canada, this is my home,” wrote another.

David Aldana immigrated from Colombia and has been following the referendum campaigns, even though he can't vote. Other Albertans with permanent residency but no Canadian citizenship also left messages on the board. (Elise Stolte/CBC)

Several people with permanent residency but not Canadian citizenship stopped by. One was David Aldana, who moved to Canada from Colombia.

“If I could vote, I would stay with Canada, and because I feel that unity is better,” he said. “I think unity is better for the country itself. I'm in love with Canada. I'm in love with the freedom that we have here.”

Concerns the vote could backfire

In Alberta, support for independence had been polling at about 27 per cent this spring , according to a poll from Janet Brown Opinion Research commissioned by CBC News.

That softened to 23 per cent in a similar poll by Janet Brown in September, which also found Premier Danielle Smith’s United Conservative Party lost some support, likely due to frustration over the vote.

One man at the library called it a nightmare. He wrote: “Talk about backfiring. Rather than more consideration from Ottawa we are now facing a potential NDP resurgence (the worst outcome you could imagine).”

On the left, a Ukrainian newcomer left her concerns: the referendum reminds her of separation votes in the Ukrainian regions of Crimea and Donbas. On the right, a public servant wrote a note about his hope for a transparent referendum process. (Elise Stolte/CBC)

Muaaz Asher is a Grade 10 student who stopped by after class at the nearby Joane Cardinal-Schubert High School. He said at school they tried to look at the separation arguments from both sides.

“Surprisingly, a lot of my class wanted to stay. And I really found that fascinating ‘cause there's just one of my friends who is heavily right. He always agrees with whatever right-wingers say but this time … he wants to stay in Canada,” Asher said.

“It kind of just shows that as a country — it sounds a bit corny, but there's a lot of love and unity. I think that's really special, and I think we just can't give that up.”

Muaaz Asher is a Grade 10 student who discussed the Alberta referendum question at school. (Elise Stolte/CBC)

'Strong opinions on both sides'

The voices for unity were loudest and most common at the library Thursday. But it’s one location, on one afternoon.

Destiny Fox stopped by and suggested you can’t judge how people in general are feeling by those most willing to speak up.

“I don't think that a lot of people are being very open about their opinion to leave Canada as honestly as people who want to stay in Canada,” Fox said. “So you're just not hearing as much … You're not going to see the lawn signs on people's personal property because they don't want to get into it with their neighbours. But I think that there are a lot of strong opinions on both sides.

“I'm glad that we're having this referendum because I feel like it's giving everybody an opportunity to voice their feelings. And I don't necessarily feel that I want to separate from Canada, but I do want the premier to have the power to go back to Ottawa and say this is how Albertans are feeling.”

World.title: Hurricane Simon hits Mexico's Pacific coast, slamming towns and resorts
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Hurricane Simon was pounding Mexico's Pacific coast as a Category 4 storm on Sunday, its eye remaining just offshore as its most powerful winds and rain slammed people living between the Sierra Madre and the ocean.

Simon's eye was moving northward just off the coast, and forecasters at the U.S. National Hurricane Center said it's not clear if it will make landfall. This could mean Simon maintains its extremely dangerous strength, sustaining winds of 240 km/h.

That's not good news for people in the Puerto Vallarta area, a popular destination for Canadian tourists. Just inland and uphill from the resort areas, many Mexicans live in communities where housing might not stand up to the storm.

At daybreak, Simon was centered about 175 kilometres south-southeast of Cabo Corrientes, and moving north-northwest at a relatively slow eight km/h. A senior Hurricane Center specialist, Phillippe Pappin, said this westernmost tip of mainland Mexico was the most likely place for landfall.

"Simon is very close to the coast of Mexico this morning," Pappin told The Associated Press on Sunday.

"We're expecting catastrophic wind and life-threatening storm surge impacts along that west central coast of Mexico where the hurricane warning is currently in effect," Pappin said.

"They're also getting very heavy rainfall associated with the storm that's likely going to produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides in areas of higher terrain along the Mexican coastline, and there will be significant swells."

As for predicting whether or not Simon will make landfall, "it's a little tricky right now" to forecast, since the eye "is basically moving very close or parallel to the coast currently," Pappin said. But he predicted that Cabo Corrientes is the area most likely to get a direct hit from the system on Sunday.

Waves hit the shore in Manzanillo on Sunday. (Daniel Becerril/Reuters)

Heavy rainfall elsewhere

Meanwhile, the hurricane was dumping rain over parts of southwestern Mexico. It could bring 25 to 50 centimetres of rain in many places, with some areas in the states of Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco receiving up to 76 centimetres. "This rainfall will produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain," the centre warned.

Jalisco state suspended classes on Friday and Monday in 22 coastal municipalities and began evacuating people from at-risk areas while asking the tourism sector to make sure workers as well as visitors are fully accommodated in shelters or safe zones.

On Saturday, just ahead of the worst weather, convenience stores, hotels and other businesses in Puerto Vallarta were boarding up their windows.

A man removes water from a building in Manzanillo on Sunday. (Daniel Becerril/Reuters)

The hurricane centre expected a dangerous storm surge along the immediate coast near and to the east of where the centre makes landfall. The agency warned that near the coast, large and destructive waves will accompany the surge.

Canadian tourist Ed Currie, who, along with his wife, still has five more days to enjoy Puerto Vallarta, said the hurricane had not yet affected his plans.

"Just stay in the hotel and look out the window hopefully," he said of what the couple would do. "I just don't know what to expect."

World.title: Saudis say Riyadh airport struck for 2nd day in a row, separate airport also attacked
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A projectile struck a passenger terminal at the international airport in Riyadh on Sunday, a day after a missile hit the same terminal and killed 12 people, the Saudi-led coalition fighting Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen said. The Houthis claimed responsibility for those attacks and others.

Saudi authorities said there were injuries in the latest attack on the King Khalid International Airport complex for terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights. Saturday's missile attack was the deadliest in a Gulf Arab nation since the Iran war began, with another 300 people wounded, some critically.

The sharp escalation in the new front in the Iran war threatens to draw in greater U.S. military involvement as U.S. President Donald Trump has said he is weighing joining the fight against the rebels.

WATCH | Saudi airport struck twice in less than 24 hours: Saudi airport targeted again 24 hours after attack left 12 dead | Duration 1:34

The Indian Embassy in Saudi Arabia said one of its citizens died Sunday of injuries sustained in Saturday's attack, which would bring the death toll to 13.

Saudi authorities later said King Fahd International Airport in Dammam also had been attacked, with few details. The city is on the Persian Gulf near Bahrain and Qatar.

The strikes came shortly after the Houthis said the airport under their control in the Yemeni capital of Sanaa had been struck again. They blamed the Saudis but provided no details.

At stake, again, are global supplies and prices of oil, as well as commercial shipping through a crucial alternative waterway to the Iran-threatened Strait of Hormuz — along with civilians and aviation throughout the region.

Trump on Saturday also said he planned to speak with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who has been seeking assistance.

A U.S. intervention could prompt the Houthis to halt shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea off Yemen and further restrict the flow of oil out of the Persian Gulf. The rebels seized key areas along the strait last month, and the Saudi-led coalition has been trying to seize them back.

Saudi Arabia is running low on missile interceptors and has asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air defence support to the region, regional officials told The Associated Press last month, with one noting that the U.S. has seen its own stock dwindle during the war with Iran.

Sunday's attack occurred as the Saudis hosted a major international energy conference in Riyadh, with other high-profile events, including an investment gathering, on the horizon. Saudi Arabia under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has sought to open more to the world as a business and tourism destination, but the Houthi attacks threaten those efforts.

"There is no way that somebody will break our back. We are like a phoenix, we come out of the ashes all the time," the Saudi energy minister, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud, told the conference.

He added that the kingdom is also working on pipelines, in addition to the East-West one that was attacked and closed for days last month, with no details.

Airports a 'theatre of operations': Houthis

Earlier Sunday, the Houthi-run Health Ministry reported that a child was killed and six people wounded in a suspected Saudi airstrike on a house in Sanaa.

The ministry says 91 Yemenis have been killed and 168 injured by the Saudi-led coalition in five weeks. It said that 60 per cent of those killed were women and children.

There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities.

WATCH | A look from 2024 on how the Houthis gained prominence: How the Houthis became major Middle East disruptors | Duration 6:51 Once a rag-tag group in Yemen — one of the world’s poorest countries — Iran has helped the Houthis become major players capable of disrupting global shipping traffic in the Red Sea. CBC’s Paul Hunter breaks down the rise of the Houthis and what the world needs to watch for. [Correction: In a previous version of this video, we reported that Hamas is considered a terrorist organization by several countries and entities, including the United Nations. In fact, the UN does not consider Hamas a terrorist organization.]

On Sunday, the Houthis claimed the attack on the airport in Dammam as well as attacks on oil and gas facilities in the kingdom's east. They have targeted the Riyadh airport, which has no military facilities, every day since Wednesday.

The rebels again warned "all airlines, experts, employees, workers and ​travellers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theatre of operations for our ​forces." Several international airlines have suspended flights for varying periods.

Saudi authorities said the dead in Saturday's attack included four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a U.S. citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese.

Relatives display a portrait of Syrian citizen Buthaina Ahmad Oweida, who they say was killed in Saturday's attack on the international airport in Riyadh. (Omar Albam/The Associated Press)

The Egyptian woman was a flight attendant identified as Azza Ramzy, 28, who worked for the Saudi airline Flynas, according to the Egyptian state-run TV.

The Syrian woman was a widowed mother of four who had been living in Saudi Arabia for five years, a relative told The Associated Press. The Syrian Embassy in Riyadh identified her as Buthaina Ahmad Oweida.

Impact on Iran war

Until recently, the Houthis had been largely on the sidelines of the Iran war. Now, the rebels are helping Iran to pressure a key U.S. ally.

The Saudis and the Houthis began fighting in 2015, when the kingdom entered Yemen's civil war on behalf of the internationally recognized government.

Relative calm after a 2022 ceasefire ended in July, when the Houthis resumed attacks, saying the Saudis fired on the Sanaa airport as a plane from Iran was trying to land. That revived anger over the Saudi-led blockade that has largely isolated Houthi-run areas.

Now fighting has escalated, with the Saudi-led coalition providing air support for Yemeni government forces attempting to reverse recent Houthi gains along the Red Sea.

Those gains gave the rebels better surveillance of shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb, a corridor that is a crucial alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has been attacking ships.

Ahmed Nagi, the International Crisis Group's senior analyst for Yemen, said the Houthi pressure tactics could backfire: "Rather than pushing Riyadh to step back, attacks on critical Saudi infrastructure could make the Saudis more determined to continue the campaign."

World.title: How good is this year's flu shot? Here's what to know about flu season
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Walking down the street this week, it may seem like everyone is sneezing and hacking up a lung. But as health officials announce the start of an earlier than usual flu season, how worried should Canadians be? And as we head into Thanksgiving weekend, should we be scrambling to update flu and COVID-19 shots?

Some experts say that while this year's flu season may have arrived on our doorstep sooner than usual, it's not necessarily a cause for alarm — but other experts are stressing the importance of prevention in heavy-hit regions such as Toronto and Calgary, where one of this season's two influenza deaths so far has occurred, according to authorities.

The strain making up roughly 98 per cent of cases in Canada so far tends to be a milder one, according to Brian Ward, professor emeritus at the Research Institute of the McGill University Health Centre in Montreal.

"So far at least, this looks like an H1N1 dominated year, and the years where H1N1 dominates, you can have very large outbreaks, but the number or the proportion of people … who get very sick, is relatively small compared to years that are dominated by H3N2," he told CBC News.

"I'm not convinced yet that we're actually seeing the beginning of a real outbreak. What we're seeing is sort of isolated, small outbreaks."

But where the flu is striking, doctors say it's striking hard. There are currently more than 400 confirmed flu cases in Alberta, where vaccines aren't yet widely available.

Some regions have started rolling out flu and COVID-19 shots to high-risk populations, with most regions set to offer shots to the general public by mid-October.

Here's what we know.

Is everyone getting sick right now?

According to the latest national numbers, which include data on influenza trends up to Oct. 3, there have been 3,315 detections of influenza across the country since the end of August. More than 1,140 of those cases were detected in the most recent week of available data, showing that cases are picking up.

Influenza has been associated with two deaths so far this flu season, national figures state. The person who died in Alberta lived in the Calgary area and was in the 70-79 age range, authorities say. Authorities haven't yet shared where the second death occurred.

It's an early start to the season. Between Sept. 27 and Oct. 3, 4.7 per cent of influenza tests came back positive, much higher than the average 0.6 per cent rate seen this time of year in 2023-2025.

But much of this national increase is driven by an uptick of cases in B.C. and in large cities such as Toronto and Calgary. Other areas seeing cases creep up include Yukon, the Northwest Territories and Alberta.

"The rest of the country is really very quiet," Ward said.

WATCH | B.C. launches fall immunization campaign: B.C. warns of early start to flu season, launches fall immunization campaign | Duration closed caption 7:05 Flu season has started early this year and the province has launched its fall immunization campaign to prevent the spread. Dr. Jennifer Vines with the B.C. Centre for Disease Control shares what the vaccine rollout will look like and what precautions people can take to stay healthy.

He noted that in B.C., outbreaks in long-term care homes are driving the increase in cases, warning that families getting together this holiday weekend could result in further spread.

"That may be the seed that moves the virus … into the schools and universities and marketplaces and so on."

Official figures don't catch every case of flu, as not everyone seeks out a test when they fall ill.

In hard-hit Toronto, family doctor Joseph Param told CBC News the increase of flu patients he's seeing at his practice is mainly among young adults who are more likely to travel on public transit and may still go to work when feeling under the weather, perhaps because they're used to flu season starting later.

WATCH | Ontario deals with earlier-than-usual flu season: You're not imagining it — flu season has started early this year | Duration closed caption 2:10 Some Ontario doctors say they're noticing an early start to this year's flu season in their waiting rooms, as influenza cases tick up across the province ahead of schedule.

"Over the last couple of weeks, patients who are very healthy who see me rarely have been coming in with severe symptoms," he said.

"So it is important that the general population is aware that we are seeing … early cases now and so that we start taking precautions earlier than expected."

Doctors advise Canadians to stay home if they feel ill and to get vaccinated as soon as shots become available in their area, particularly with the long weekend coming up.

How effective is the flu shot this year?

The protection of flu shots varies from year to year depending on the most dominant strain of influenza in your area.

This year, it's a "good" match, Ward said. Although H3N2 viruses dominated for much of 2025, that subtype hasn't cropped up much in 2026, and this year's vaccine is well-positioned to protect against H1N1.

He said "influenza viruses march to their own drummers" and can mutate even within one flu season.

It's not just flu season in Canada — historically, we see more respiratory illnesses in general cropping up during the fall and going into winter, including colds and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), the latter of which is most dangerous in young children.

About 98 per cent of lab-confirmed cases of influenza in Canada since the end of August have been of the H1N1 strain, according to government data. (New Africa/Shutterstock)

Rates of COVID-19 are currently trending lower right now than last year, with 4.1 per cent of tests coming back positive in the last week of September compared with 10.5 per cent at the same time in 2025.

The National Advisory Committee on Immunizations (NACI) said in September that it continues to "strongly recommend" the latest COVID-19 booster shots for those at a higher risk of developing severe COVID-19, including health-care workers, adults over the age of 65, those with immunocompromised systems and people in long-term care homes.

When can I get my flu and COVID-19 shots?

Several provinces such as Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia are already advising residents that appointments for flu vaccines and COVID-19 booster shots are available now for residents over the age of six months.

New Brunswick , Saskatchewan and Manitoba are currently allowing residents to book their flu and COVID-19 vaccines, with immunization efforts officially kicking off on Oct. 13.

Those living in Newfoundland and Labrador can receive flu and COVID-19 shots starting Oct. 19.

In Ontario, flu and COVID-19 immunizations have been available since last week for high-risk groups, including seniors aged 65 and up, hospitalized patients, long-term care residents and health-care workers, according to the provincial government. They don't open to the general public until Oct. 26 .

In Quebec, you can start making appointments as of Oct. 13, but the flu and COVID-19 vaccination campaign itself doesn't begin until Oct. 20 . It is only free to eligible residents deemed high-risk, meaning non-eligible residents must pay for the shots.

Flu and COVID-19 shots can be booked now in Alberta , with the first appointments starting Oct. 19. While flu shots are free to everyone, Albertans who aren't considered high-risk for COVID-19 will have to pay.

In B.C., those registered in their Get Vaccinated system will receive a notification reminding them to get their flu shots. Flu and COVID-19 shots are available starting Oct. 13.

COVID-19 and flu shots will be available at specific clinics in the Northwest Territories this fall, but a timeline hasn't been released yet. Those in Yukon have been able to book appointments for flu and COVID-19 shots since the end of September. No details have been released for Nunavut's rollout as of Oct. 8.

Before heading out to the pharmacy or clinic, it's important to check the requirements in your area to be sure you're eligible and that providers near you have received the necessary supplies to offer shots and aren't experiencing delays.

Most regions offer RSV vaccines to eligible patients as well.

In the future, we could see more variety in our flu vaccines: an mRNA influenza vaccine made by Moderna was approved by the FDA in the U.S. in the summer, making this the first flu season it'll face. It's still under review by Health Canada.

World.title: Support floods in for Gus, Halifax's 104-year-old gopher tortoise, ahead of surgery
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A beloved 104-year-old gopher tortoise, Gus, is receiving love and well wishes from supporters across the world ahead of his surgery.

Jeff Gray, the manager of the Museum of Natural History in Halifax, where Gus resides, says hundreds of letters, get-well cards and pieces of art have been sent to the tortoise in the two weeks since it was announced he is to undergo surgery Tuesday for a bladder stone. The museum's social media accounts have also received thousands of messages from people across Canada and beyond who are wishing Gus well.

"It's just so lovely that people have this sort of universal experience with Gus … people who visited Gus when they were a child, they return with their children, they return with their grandchildren," Gray said in an interview Friday.

"I think the nostalgia … being able to have that experience and share that with your children or grandchildren is something that really resonates with people," he added.

Gus is believed to be the oldest gopher tortoise in the world.

He has been a part of the Museum of Natural History since 1942, when a former museum director bought him for $5 in Florida. He is believed to have hatched in 1922.

Almost every day, visitors can join Gus on his afternoon walk around the museum. He strolls in the museum's grassy yard when the weather is warm, and wanders around the exhibits indoors when it's cold or rainy.

He can often be seen basking under a heat lamp in his sandy enclosure.

Gus will be taking a break from his public walks as he recovers in the museum in private for several weeks after surgery. (The Canadian Press)

During Friday afternoon's walk, about 20 visitors watched the tortoise munch on strawberries, lettuce and a banana. Among them were Becky Cooper and her eight-year-old son, Spike Cooper, who were visiting from Maine.

"I have a new idol. Someone I want to emulate when I'm 104," Becky Cooper said with a laugh.

Spike Cooper said he had never seen a tortoise before, and he was impressed by Gus.

"I think that he's really good … I hope that he's going to take [the surgery] well," the eight-year-old said.

The Coopers were in town to see their friend, Hannah Doktor, who lives in the Halifax area and visits Gus often. Doktor said she learned about Gus and his daily walks the first week she moved to the city, and she's been a devoted fan ever since.

"I saw him and I thought, 'Yeah. I'd die for him,'" Doktor said of Gus.

Gus will be taking a break from his public walks as he recovers in the museum in private for several weeks after surgery.

Gray said Gus's veterinary team first became aware of a bladder stone in 2009, and a more recent scan showed the stone has grown and is now pressing on nearby tissue.

In 2009, operating on the stone would have involved drilling through his shell, Gray said. But now, veterinary surgical advancements mean the stone can be removed through a small incision in Gus's leg.

"There's a fear that if we don't do something and the bladder stone continues to grow, it will start to push against other organs and start to cause discomfort," Gray said. "He's certainly not showing any signs of pain now."

For Carolyn Koslowski and Pia Pirzer, two university students on exchange from Germany, Friday marked their first time meeting Gus. Both said they were blown away by how cute he is.

Pirzer said it was her mother in Germany who urged her to visit the beloved tortoise. She said Gus came up in her mother's research about things to see in Halifax.

"My mom has been telling me about him for weeks. And finally we made it to see him," Pirzer said.

"We really hope that he's going to do well in his surgery. We know he is strong," Koslowski said.

Gray said bladder stones are relatively common in tortoises, and there's evidence the procedure he'll receive has been successful for other gopher tortoises. What's uncommon is a veterinary surgery on a reptile that's more than 100 years old.

In the wild, gopher tortoises typically live about 60 years.

Because of Gus's age, "we tend to worry in general about going into these things. But he is in great health, and tortoises that have been in great health have had great results," Gray said.

Outside of captivity, these tortoises' lives are typically cut short due to human interference, Gray said. They're vulnerable to being struck by vehicles and development that encroaches on their habitats.

"Conversely, in captivity, where humans can provide them with a secure environment, regular diet and veterinary visits, that tends to prolong a lifespan," he said.

Gray said all surgeries come with risk, but museum staff and Gus's veterinary team believe the procedure will give him the best chance at a healthy and comfortable future.

Gus's daily walks will continue as usual throughout this weekend and on Monday, which will be his last public stroll before his surgery on Tuesday.
