Salome Zourabichvili herself should answer the remaining questions. What matters is that the state is responding to this issue,” Papuashvili said.

He added, however, that he could not go into the details of the investigation.

It has emerged, however, that the parliament speaker, like current Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, voted in parliament in favour of appointing Nana Keinishvili to the National Bank of Georgia’s Council.

Details of the case

According to the National Bank, it reviewed submissions from the management of Bitexchange LLC and conducted a preliminary internal investigation within the scope of its authority.

The materials were forwarded to the relevant authorities for legal assessment, as the matter falls outside the mandate established for the National Bank by law. The bank expressed hope that the facts of the case would be established objectively as soon as possible.

The bank also explained that Bitexchange, a virtual asset service provider, had been fined following a routine inspection for violating anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing regulations.

Nana Keinishvili

According to the Prosecutor’s Office, the management of Bitexchange claims that Keinishvili is involved in business activities and directly controls a network of companies subject to regulation by the National Bank.

They allege that shares in these companies are registered in the names of her family members and affiliated individuals. The company’s management also claims that Keinishvili attempted to acquire a stake in their business.

The Prosecutor’s Office notes that Georgia’s Law on the Fight Against Corruption prohibits public officials from engaging in business activities. Furthermore, under the Organic Law on the National Bank of Georgia, members of the National Bank’s Council and their family members are prohibited from being partners in a Georgian financial sector entity or a legal entity affiliated with one.

According to the Prosecutor’s Office, the investigation will examine the circumstances surrounding Nana Keinishvili’s possible unlawful involvement in business activities. The public will be informed of the results of the investigation in due course.

Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty investigation

The National Bank has not disclosed the amount of the fine. However, according to the investigation by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, Nana Keinishvili demanded a stake in a cryptocurrency company regulated by the National Bank. The company’s owner refused to give up a share, after which the National Bank fined the company 572 million lari (approximately $211.85 million).

The investigation also found that Keinishvili and her family members own and manage profitable businesses regulated by the National Bank.

Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty obtained documents indicating that the National Bank and the State Security Service had been aware of information about Keinishvili’s alleged violations for at least several months. Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty sent inquiries to both agencies on 6 October.

News in Georgia

World.title: Georgia’s Communications Commission bans two TV channels from using 93 words and phrases
World.content:
Georgia’s National Communications Commission has banned the critical TV channels Formula and TV Pirveli from using 93 words and phrases.

The list includes “regime”, “political prisoners”, “prisoners of conscience”, “oligarch”, “repressive laws” and “judicial clan”.

Transparency International Georgia (TI) believes the Commission is using content regulation mechanisms to punish critical media outlets and undermine their financial position.

According to information published by TI, the Communications Commission has issued seven official reports over the past six months. Four concerned Formula TV and three concerned TV Pirveli. The Commission initially gave the broadcasters verbal warnings, then fined each of them 2,500 lari ($926) for the first offence and 5,000 lari ($1,852) for the next. On 1 October, it imposed an additional fine of 10,000 lari ($3,704) on Formula TV.

TI warns that TV Pirveli could face a similar fine if the Commission continues along the same lines. The organisation notes that the Commission fines the broadcasters in turn, while the financial penalties place an additional burden on TV channels already operating under difficult economic conditions.

TI is particularly concerned that the Commission also has the power to suspend broadcasting licences. The organisation believes that the use of these powers could pose a serious threat to the operations of critical TV channels.

Where is the line between impartiality and censorship?

The Communications Commission mainly accuses the TV channels of violating the principle of impartiality by covering current affairs through the lens of journalists’ personal attitudes and opinions. It uses these allegations to justify its demand that broadcasters refrain from using certain words and expressions.

Transparency International Georgia examined all seven reports prepared by the Commission. It found that the Commission had deemed 33 words and phrases unacceptable for TV Pirveli and 68 for Formula. Some expressions appear on both lists, bringing the total number of banned words and phrases to 93.

However, the organisation says the Commission’s demands go beyond the use of individual words. According to the reports, broadcasters must also present news in a form stripped of as much evaluation and analysis as possible.

In one example, a journalist discusses the creation of an informal movement backed by the authorities and calls it a “morality police”. In another report, a journalist claims that the Georgian authorities have copied the Chechen model, under which officials give athletes an official mandate and allow them to use violence.

The expressions deemed unacceptable by the Commission also include phrases about the detention of activists, a visit by ruling party representatives to Washington and Georgia’s EU accession process. In one of the reports that prompted sanctions, a journalist accuses the authorities of spreading disinformation. The journalist also says the government blames Europe’s policies for the suspension of Georgia’s European integration instead of taking responsibility for its own decisions.

The Commission argues that such wording reflects the broadcaster’s personal attitude and opinion. It says this violates the requirement for impartiality when covering public policy issues, as set out in Article 54(5) of Georgia’s Law on Broadcasting.

Monitoring pro-government channels and the political context

Transparency International says the Commission threatened critical broadcasters with monitoring after the UK imposed sanctions on the pro-government TV channels Imedi and POSTV on 24 February 2026.

The UK cited the deliberate spread of false information about Russia’s war against Ukraine and support for Russian disinformation as grounds for the sanctions.

The Communications Commission also placed the pro-government channels Imedi, POSTV and Rustavi 2 under monitoring. However, Transparency International argues that this process is largely a formality designed to make the Commission appear impartial, while the authorities direct actual pressure at independent media.

The organisation also raises concerns about the Commission’s membership and independence. According to TI, the fact that some commissioners are loyal to or have ties to the ruling Georgian Dream party raises further doubts about the impartiality of the decisions they make.

Media financial sustainability under threat

Fines against critical TV channels are increasing even as the broadcasters struggle with difficult financial conditions. Repeated penalties and the possibility of licence suspension make their ability to continue operating an even more pressing concern.

Transparency International argues that the Communications Commission should not act as a censor or use its powers to punish media outlets for criticising the authorities. In TI’s view, media self-regulation should take precedence when the Commission considers disputed journalistic content. The Commission’s main role should be to support self-regulation, rather than punish broadcasters for criticising the government and exposing its representatives.

World.title: Armenian AI factory rejects Russian allegations of intelligence gathering
World.content:
Firebird AI rejects Russian espionage allegations

“Claims circulating about Firebird AI’s activities are untrue and have no factual basis,” the Armenia-based company Firebird AI said in response to remarks by Alexei Shevtsov, deputy secretary of Russia’s Security Council.

On 8 August 2026, Firebird AI opened the first AI factory in the city of Hrazdan. It is the largest data centre in the region and plans to expand its operations further. The facility already uses more than 6,000 NVIDIA Blackwell B200/B300 graphics processing units (GPUs). By the end of 2027, the company plans to deploy more than 70,000 NVIDIA Blackwell and Vera Rubin chips. The project has received around $500 million in initial investment. Total investment could reach $4 billion or more.

The Russian official claimed that this powerful data centre could be used for espionage: “Such centres could support analytical and intelligence operations on behalf of Western intelligence agencies, including against Iran, Russia and countries in the South Caucasus and Central Asia.”

This is not the first time Alexei Shevtsov has criticised projects under way in Armenia. Around the same time, he also expressed concern about the Armenian-American TRIPP initiative, known as the “Trump Route”, which aims to unblock regional transport links. According to Shevtsov, the project could lead to the deployment of US private military companies and intelligence infrastructure in Armenia.

“The computing capacity is used exclusively for civilian purposes”

Firebird AI said its AI factory is a technology company that develops and operates high-performance computing infrastructure.

“The US export licence issued to the company restricts the use of the relevant computing capacity exclusively to civilian purposes.”

Firebird AI’s management said the Russian Security Council deputy secretary’s claims showed a lack of understanding of how AI computing infrastructure operates.

“The geographical location of these services does not, in itself, determine the nature or purpose of their use.”

What concerns Russia

Alexei Shevtsov said that Firebird AI’s US jurisdiction could allow US intelligence agencies to access all the data stored on its servers.

“This means that data belonging to Armenian government agencies, companies and citizens could become accessible to the United States without the consent of the Armenian authorities.”

However, the main concern centres on the possibility that the data centre could gather intelligence. This could allegedly affect not only Russia’s interests but also those of Iran, for example.

The Russian Security Council representative then turned to Armenia’s energy capacity.

“According to announced plans, Firebird intends to increase the capacity of its Hrazdan complex to 300 MW by the end of 2027. This represents almost a quarter of Armenia’s winter peak electricity demand of 1.3 GW. The announced plans will require additional generating capacity to keep the centre running.”

This issue concerns Russia because Armenia plans to build a new nuclear power plant, and Russia hopes to secure the contract. Russia built the existing Metsamor nuclear power plant. Against this backdrop, Shevtsov questioned the need to diversify Armenia’s partnerships in the nuclear energy sector.

Armenia may instead opt for the small modular reactors that the United States has offered, as previously discussed. In that case, Shevtsov said:

“I would like to emphasise that the United States has not built and is not building any small modular reactors abroad. Meanwhile, Rosatom is currently building 30 power units abroad, including small modular reactors. The choice, as they say, is obvious.”

Firebird AI rejects Russian espionage allegations

World.title: ‘Civil society has the right to participate safely’: OSCE chair responds to Georgian authorities
World.content:
At the OSCE Human Dimension Conference in Warsaw, a representative of Switzerland, the organisation’s chair for 2026, said that the Chairpersonship was concerned about remarks made by the authorities in Georgia regarding the participation of Georgian civil society representatives in the conference, as well as information received from human rights defenders.

The Swiss representative’s statement followed comments by Georgian Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili about NGO representatives attending the conference in Warsaw. On 7 October, Papuashvili said he did not understand how they had paid for the trip or who was funding them:

“How do they pay for these trips, and who funds them? These organisations are not registered in the transparency register. If they do not disclose [the source of their income] to the state, it means they are funded by ‘black money’. This is further evidence that organisations in Georgia receive ‘black money’, including from various European institutions,” the speaker said.

What did the Swiss representative say?

“Providing a platform where civil society representatives can participate and engage with OSCE participating States and executive structures is one of the OSCE’s core values. They must be able to do so without facing any negative consequences.

This is essential for the OSCE’s mechanisms to function. We are concerned about comments made in connection with the participation of Georgian civil society representatives in this conference, as well as reports received from various human rights defenders attending the OSCE Human Dimension Conference in Warsaw. We reiterate the importance of ensuring safe participation in OSCE events, without any reprisals.”

Incident at the conference

The conference in Warsaw is attended by Baia Pataraia, head of the Georgian NGO Sapari, and Tamar Oniani, head of the Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association.

On 5 October, during a speech by a representative of the Georgian delegation, Pataraia held up a banner reading: “Free all Georgian political prisoners.”

Pataraia says her protest was peaceful and silent, and that she had arranged it in advance in accordance with OSCE rules.

“Wherever I find myself alongside the [Georgian] government, I will remind them that prisons are full of political prisoners and that the Georgian people will never accept this,” she says.

Pataraia adds that Germany, Slovenia and other countries have urged Georgia to implement the recommendations of the Moscow Mechanism and stop persecuting media representatives, politicians and civil society members.

In this context, she also criticised the Georgian authorities’ bid to make Georgia the OSCE chair in 2027.

“They want benefits, money, prestige and power from everyone, but they themselves fulfil none of their obligations,” Pataraia said indignantly.

The ruling Georgian Dream party is seeking to secure the OSCE chairpersonship for 2027. Georgian Foreign Minister Maka Bochorishvili says the country has already submitted its application to the OSCE and hopes to win the support of participating States. However, according to the publication Rapporteur, EU member states do not support Georgia’s bid.



OSCE conference in Warsaw

World.title: Abkhazia plans pension reform, new law to take work history into account
World.content:
The government of Abkhazia has drafted a pension reform bill aimed at streamlining pension legislation, taking employment history into account when calculating pension payments and introducing specific support measures for socially vulnerable groups.

The draft pension law was prepared by the Ministry of Social Welfare and Demographic Policy. According to Minister Kama Adzynba, the bill aims to streamline regulations governing employment-related, insurance-based and funded pensions, as well as payments for special services to the country.

One of the key principles of the proposed reform is to take individuals’ employment history into account when determining pension payments. Currently, pensions in Abkhazia stand at 6,000 roubles [approximately $70], a standard amount paid to everyone, regardless of whether they have worked for many years or have never been formally employed.

Pensioners who hold dual Abkhaz-Russian citizenship and also receive a Russian pension have their Abkhaz pension reduced to a largely symbolic 500 roubles [around $6].

The new system is intended to address this “injustice”. It also provides for survivor’s pensions and other social benefits, which are expected to exceed the basic social pension.

The bill also introduces special pensions for distinguished service to the country. Recipients of state orders and veterans of the 1992-93 Georgian-Abkhaz war are among those proposed for inclusion in this category.

The draft law will be submitted to parliament for consideration.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Azerbaijan’s $90bn reserves draw criticism from former opposition leader
World.content:
Azerbaijan’s foreign currency reserves

Ilgar Mammadov, former chairman of Azerbaijan’s Republican Alternative (ReAl) party, has criticised the country’s accumulation of $90bn in foreign currency reserves. In a Facebook post, he argued that there was little reason to take pride in such substantial reserves when some elderly citizens were forced to survive on modest social benefits.

Mammadov proposed using part of the reserves to improve living standards while expanding economic freedoms.

“There are no reasonable grounds for a country like Azerbaijan to hold $90bn in foreign currency reserves,” the politician wrote.

What makes up Azerbaijan’s $90bn in foreign currency reserves?

Azerbaijan’s strategic foreign currency reserves comprise the Central Bank’s foreign exchange reserves and the assets of the State Oil Fund (SOFAZ). According to figures published by the State Statistical Committee, their combined value stood at $90.77bn as of 1 September 2026. This represents the total value of funds held in various financial assets.

The two institutions’ reserves serve different purposes. The Central Bank’s reserves are used to maintain stability in the foreign exchange market and mitigate risks associated with external payments.

The State Oil Fund accumulates revenues from oil and gas production, invests them, makes transfers to the state budget and builds up savings for future generations. Its assets are invested in bonds, equities, gold and property.

The authorities regard the substantial reserves as an indicator of the country’s financial resilience. Speaking at the Azerbaijan International Investment Forum in September, President Ilham Aliyev stressed that the reserves were approximately 20 times greater than the country’s external public debt.

According to Aliyev, this demonstrates the strength of Azerbaijan’s financial system and the stability of its national currency.

‘These $90bn have become a symbol of shame and disgrace’

Mammadov also approaches the issue from the perspective of public welfare. He argues that elderly citizens have contributed to the creation of national wealth not only through formal employment but also through domestic and agricultural work.

“Only the government of the New Azerbaijan Party (YAP) can proudly boast of having $90bn in foreign currency reserves in a country where 180,000 elderly citizens receive no retirement pension and are forced to make do with an old-age allowance of $130. This is simply shameful.

“People over the age of 65 have contributed to society throughout their lives through their labour and their role as consumers in the economy, helping to create the conditions for accumulating $90bn in foreign currency reserves.

“Whether it was a housewife who spent years supporting her husband as he worked as a labourer or engineer, or a man who worked in the fields for a pittance, supplying city residents with fresh fruit and vegetables, they all contributed to building up these reserves.

“This is a hardworking generation that the YAP authorities have left with virtually no means of subsistence in old age, while continuing to boast about the country’s foreign currency reserves.”

Mammadov argues that taking pride in growing reserves while this generation faces financial hardship is also morally unacceptable.

“Viewed from this perspective, even the question of economic efficiency becomes secondary. These $90bn have become a symbol of shame and disgrace.”

Assets held abroad and dependence on oil

Mammadov also argues that holding substantial foreign currency reserves abroad carries political risks. He cites Iraq and Libya as examples, pointing to the depletion of their financial resources during wars and the freezing of their assets. He links these events to the interests of external powers and suggests that Azerbaijan could face similar risks.

“By maintaining foreign currency reserves on this scale, Azerbaijan is merely provoking major players in the current world order, who are accustomed to playing by their own rules. It is like putting on our most expensive jacket, stuffing its pockets with bundles of cash and going for a walk at night down the most crime-ridden street in the city.

“There are plenty of historical examples. In 1980, Iraq’s foreign currency reserves stood at 36bn–40bn. In today’s money, that is just over $90bn. And what happened? A war with Iran was soon orchestrated, partly for the sake of that money, though not exclusively. As a result, all the money was spent on purchasing weapons from abroad, and the reserves were exhausted. Who benefited? The arms dealers.

“In 2011, Libya’s foreign currency reserves had barely reached $150bn when the country was plunged into turmoil. Some of the money was spent on arming the sides in the civil war, while around a third of the assets were frozen in foreign financial institutions (and someone is still profiting from them). The rest has never been traced.

“In today’s world, where the law of the jungle prevails, there is no point in keeping such substantial foreign currency reserves abroad. One day, a provocation could be staged against us too, and the money could be seized,” he wrote.

Mammadov also sees a potential collapse in financial markets as a serious threat. He believes securities are significantly overvalued and that a sharp fall in their prices could result in substantial losses for Azerbaijan.

Another of his arguments concerns the economy’s dependence on oil. Recalling the currency devaluations of 2015, he notes that the country’s foreign currency reserves failed to prevent the sharp depreciation of the manat.

“The reason reserves are rapidly depleted during a crisis and cannot serve as a financial safety net lies in the unhealthy state of our economy and its dependence on oil.”

According to Mammadov, if oil prices remain low for a prolonged period, substantial foreign currency reserves alone cannot guarantee economic security.

What does Mammadov propose?

Mammadov is not calling for Azerbaijan to spend all its foreign currency reserves. He believes some funds should be retained to deal with economic crises and natural disasters, although he does not specify how much should be set aside.

“There is an urgent need to improve people’s living standards, particularly those of the elderly. At the same time, economic freedoms must be expanded without delay so that citizens can realise their creative and entrepreneurial potential and generate new wealth,” the politician wrote.

Mammadov sees the rule of law as a fundamental prerequisite for these reforms. He concluded his post by urging voters to support the Republican Alternative (ReAl) party.

World.title: Pashinyan on extradition of Azerbaijani soldier, meeting Aliyev and Medvedev’s statement
World.content:
Pashinyan on Azerbaijani serviceman’s extradition and other issues

The extradition of Azerbaijani serviceman Nasimi Musayev is not under discussion, and Baku has not made such a request. Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan told journalists this during his traditional hour-long briefing.

“What extradition are you talking about? There is no such issue, and we are not discussing it. Azerbaijan has made no request,” he said.

At the same time, he stressed that Armenia would have returned Musayev on the same day if he had not committed a crime.

Pashinyan described the Azerbaijani serviceman, who illegally crossed into Armenia and shot a resident of the village of Shaki, as having committed an “ordinary crime”. The prime minister drew parallels with other forms of cross-border crime:

“We also have other cases of cross-border crime. Drugs are constantly exported to Armenia and transported through Armenia in transit. There is no need to turn this into an apocalypse.”

The prime minister does not believe the incident in Shaki could threaten the peace process between Armenia and Azerbaijan.

He considers the peace that Armenia and Azerbaijan have established an achievement that requires protection. He warns that they could destroy it in a day, while reaching the current state of relations could take another 30 years. For this reason, he does not consider it appropriate to make statements that could threaten the peace process.

On 1 October 2026, Nasimi Musayev illegally entered the village of Shaki in Armenia’s Syunik Province. Local residents found him inside a house, where he opened fire with an assault rifle and wounded a 39-year-old woman. Her three children witnessed the incident. Her two sons also suffered injuries, while her daughter has yet to recover psychologically.

Musayev fled after the shooting, but authorities detained him shortly afterwards in another house. The Armenian Prosecutor’s Office brought criminal charges under five articles of the Criminal Code. The charges include illegally crossing the border, causing serious bodily harm to a local resident and violating the inviolability of a home. A court ordered his detention for two months.

During the briefing, the prime minister also addressed Dmitry Medvedev’s controversial statement about turning Armenia into a “new Ukraine”, a possible meeting with Aliyev at the CIS summit and the issue of missing persons.

“No official meetings are planned”: on contacts with Putin and Aliyev

On 8-9 October, Pashinyan will attend the CIS summit in Turkmenistan. Asked about possible meetings with the presidents of Russia and Azerbaijan, he recalled that his latest meetings with Putin and Aliyev took place in Bishkek last month. He also spoke to the Russian president by phone the day before.

“The format is such that contacts with the president of Russia and the president of Azerbaijan will certainly take place. We will be in the same place today and tomorrow. No official meeting is planned. If it turns out that such a meeting is necessary, it may take place,” he said.

“Armenia has already faced such a threat”: response to Medvedev

People in Armenia continue to discuss Russian Security Council Deputy Chairman Dmitry Medvedev’s statement. He said that Armenia’s leadership had decided to change the country’s course and that this would not lead to anything good.

“The worst thing that could happen to Armenia is for it to turn into a new Ukraine,” Medvedev said.

Journalists asked Pashinyan whether Armenia could face such a threat. He replied:

“Armenia has already faced a similar danger and situation. In September 2022, [during the Azerbaijani armed forces’ invasion of Armenia’s sovereign territory], the CSTO failed to fulfil its obligations.”

The Collective Security Treaty Organisation is a military alliance led by Russia. Armenia is a member of the CSTO. Under the organisation’s charter, its allies had to provide military assistance to a member state, but that did not happen.

The Armenian prime minister could not explain why Medvedev was making such statements and threats:

“Following the same logic, someone else could say: ‘We do not want Armenia to turn into a “new Russia”, given that explosions can be heard in various parts of Russia.’ This is an unfortunate genre.”

He assured that Armenia would not turn into anything else and would instead become an even more independent state.

“Some circles in Azerbaijan use this issue for political purposes”: on missing persons

Azerbaijan periodically demands that Armenia provide information about the fate of missing Azerbaijanis and the locations of their graves. President Ilham Aliyev repeated the demand at an international conference on missing persons in Baku.

According to Armenia’s prime minister, both sides should make joint efforts to establish the fate of missing people:

“We have stated that we are ready to cooperate. The problem is that some circles in Azerbaijan use this issue for political purposes, including to generate hostile rhetoric and pursue other aims.”

According to figures Pashinyan presented, the whereabouts of around 1,000 people who went missing during wars since the 1990s remain unknown in Armenia.

He says the wording itself — “their whereabouts are unknown” — shows how little information the authorities have about these people:

“Some circles in Azerbaijan sometimes try to create the impression that we know where these people are and refuse to share the information. But that is not the case.”

Pashinyan believes the two sides should resolve the issue through cooperation and close this chapter. He said that in Bishkek, he and the Azerbaijani president also discussed stepping up joint efforts by the relevant commissions of the two countries.

Pashinyan on Azerbaijani serviceman’s extradition and other issues

World.title: Iran's Hormozgan ports handle 3.84M tons of cargo in six months
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 12. A total of 3.84 million metric tons of oil and non-oil products were shipped through the ports in the western part of Hormozgan Province, located in southern Iran, during the first six months of the current Iranian year (March 21 through September 22, 2026).

According to the Iranian Ports and Maritime Organization, this was announced by Amin Sadeghi, director of the Ports Authority in the western part of Iran’s Hormozgan Province.

"Of the cargo loaded and unloaded at ports in the western part of Hormozgan Province, 2.49 million metric tons were non-oil products and 1.34 million metric tons were petroleum products," he noted.

Sadeghi also stated that during the first six months, 1.27 million metric tons of petroleum and non-oil products were exported through the ports in the western part of the province. During that period, 1.04 million metric tons of non-oil products and 230,000 metric tons of petroleum products were exported.

Moreover, the official stated that 1.75 million metric tons of oil and non-oil products were transported via coastal shipping over the six months.

"Over the past six months, 62,900 TEU containers with a total weight of approximately 644,000 metric tons were loaded and unloaded at ports in the western part of Hormozgan Province. During this period, approximately 31,500 TEU containers with a total weight of 322,000 metric tons were exported through these ports," he noted.

According to him, over the past six months, 89,900 metric tons of oil and non-oil products, as well as 46,100 passenger cars, passed through the ports in the western part of Hormozgan Province. The passenger cars were shipped to Iraq and Central Asian countries.

Sadeghi noted that over the past six months, 11,800 cargo ships called at ports in the western part of Hormozgan Province. Of these, 1,410 had a capacity of more than 1,000 metric tons, while more than 10,000 had a capacity of less than 1,000 metric tons.

According to Trend's calculation, based on information from the Iranian Ports and Maritime Organization, during the first six months of the previous Iranian year (March 21 through September 22, 2025), a total of 3.68 million metric tons of oil and non-oil products were exported from ports located in the western part of Hormozgan Province. The volume of non-oil products exported amounted to 2.06 million metric tons, while the volume of oil products was 1.62 million metric tons.

Meanwhile, 10 ports are operating in the western part of Iran’s Hormozgan Province. Among them, the busiest are the ports of Lengeh, Charak, Siri, and Lavan.

World.title: Iran's Sistan and Baluchestan customs record $110M exports
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 12. Product exports through the Chabahar, Pishin, and Rimdan customs offices in Iran's southeastern Sistan and Baluchestan Province totaled 809,000 tons, valued at $110 million, during the first six months of the current Iranian year (March 21 through September 22, 2026).

The Iran Customs Administration reported this, citing Reza Ghorbani, director general of Chabahar Customs.

Exports through the Chabahar, Pishin, and Rimdan customs offices increased by 59% in value but decreased by 9% in volume during the six months compared with the same period last year (March 21 through September 22, 2025), Ghorbani said.

"Additionally, goods from other parts of the country totaling 624,000 tons and worth $355 million were exported via the Chabahar, Pishin, and Rimdan customs offices," he said.

Ghorbani added that the main products exported through the three customs offices during the six-month period included liquefied gas, bitumen, cement, ceramics, food products, and vegetables.

He also said that 1.6 million tons of goods worth $1.23 billion were imported into the country through the three customs offices during the same period. Imports increased by 28% in value and 57% in volume compared with the same period last year.

According to Trend's analysis based on data from the Iran Customs Administration, 2.37 million tons of goods worth $352 million were exported through the customs offices of Sistan and Baluchestan Province during the first 10 months of the previous Iranian year (March 21, 2025 through January 20, 2026).

Exports increased by 39% in value and 14% in volume compared with the same period of the preceding Iranian year (March 20, 2024 through January 19, 2025).

During the first four months of the current Iranian year (March 21 through July 22, 2026), 713,000 tons of goods worth $108 million were exported through the customs offices of Sistan and Baluchestan Province. Exports increased by 61% in value and 3% in volume compared with the same period last year.

World.title: Chronicles of Victory: October 12, 2020
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 12. The Azerbaijani Army launched a counter-offensive operation, later called the "Iron Fist", on September 27, 2020, in response to the large-scale provocation of the Armenian armed forces along the frontline.

The erupted 44-day Second Karabakh War ended with the liberation of Azerbaijan’s territories from nearly 30-year Armenian occupation.

Trend presents the chronicle of the 16th day of the Second Karabakh war:

- President Ilham Aliyev gave an interview to the Turkish Haber Global TV channel.

- The territory of Aghdam district came under fire from the Armenian Armed Forces. The commander and large manpower of the forces were killed.

- As a result of an exploded shell in the village of Kangarli, Tartar district, Firudin Baylarov (born 1970) was seriously injured and hospitalized.

- The Azerbaijani Defense Ministry shared a video of the destruction of three Armenian UAVs.

- Mobile support points for the Azerbaijani troops participating in the hostilities were created.

- The Azerbaijani Defense Ministry shared a video from the liberated village of Suleymanly, Jabrayil district.

- The death toll as a result of missile attacks on Ganja city by Armenia reached 10 people.

World.title: Azerbaijani boxer becomes European champion
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 11. Another Azerbaijani boxer has won gold at the European U-17 Championships in Budva.

Mahammadali Istamov (57 kg) claimed the title after defeating England’s John Elam 4:1 on points in the final (29:28, 30:27, 28:29, 29:28, 29:28).

With this result, the Azerbaijani team concluded the U-17 European Championships with eight medals: two gold, three silver, and three bronze.

Before Istamov, Jamila Muradli (57 kg) won gold, Hasrat Mammadov (46 kg), Ismayil Nasirzade (52 kg), and Sama Abbasova (66 kg) claimed silver, while Gardash Rahimov (54 kg), Hidayat Mammadov (70 kg), and Khumar Jafarli (+80 kg) earned bronze medals.

A total of 473 athletes, including 314 boys and 159 girls, from 40 countries competed in the championship.

World.title: Azerbaijan boosts oil exports to Greece by 22%
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 11. Azerbaijan exported 284,400 tons of oil and oil products obtained from bituminous minerals to Greece worth $182.8 million in January–August 2026.

According to foreign trade customs statistics published by the State Customs Committee, the figure increased by $53.8 million, or 41.7%, in value terms and by 52,000 tons, or 22.4%, in volume terms compared with the same period of 2025, according to Trend’s calculations based on the data.

During the reporting period, Greece ranked tenth among countries importing Azerbaijani oil.

In January–August 2025, Azerbaijan exported 232,400 tons of oil and oil products obtained from bituminous minerals to Greece worth $129 million.

According to the State Customs Committee, Azerbaijan exported 368,700 tons of oil and oil products obtained from bituminous minerals to Greece worth $224.3 million in 2024, while exports amounted to 702,400 tons worth $367.7 million in 2025.

Exports in 2024–2025 showed significant growth in both physical volume and value. Supply volumes increased 1.9 times, while export value rose 1.6 times.

Specifically, export volumes increased from 368,700 tons to 702,400 tons, or 1.9 times, while export value rose from $224.3 million to $367.7 million, or 1.6 times.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s annual inflation slows to 9.3% in September
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 11. Kazakhstan’s annual inflation slowed to 9.3% in September 2026, down from 9.8% in August, according to the Bureau of National Statistics of Kazakhstan.

Inflation amounted to 0.6% month-on-month in September, unchanged from the previous month.

"Prices for food products increased by 8.5% year-on-year (9.5% in August 2026), non-food products – by 11% (11.4% in August 2026), paid services – by 8.9% (8.9% in August 2026)," the statistics bureau said.

Food and non-alcoholic beverages made the largest contribution to annual inflation, accounting for 3.2 percentage points. Personal care, social protection, other goods and services, as well as clothing and footwear each contributed 1 percentage point.

According to the Bureau, prices for some vegetables and food products declined over the month. Onion prices fell by 20.7%, lemons by 13.9%, carrots by 13.6%, potatoes by 13.4%, eggplants by 11.2%, cabbage by 10.1%, sweet peppers by 6.5%, apples by 5.3%, pears by 2.4%, garlic by 1.3% and bananas by 0.7%. Prices for baby cereals decreased by 6.1%, while granulated sugar fell by 1.3%.

In September, prices for non-food products increased by 1.1% month-on-month, while paid services rose by 1%. Food prices declined by 0.1%.

Among non-food products, prices fell for hand cream by 6.9%, children's diapers by 6.6%, televisions by 5.6%, dishwashers and microwave ovens by 1.8% each, and shower gel by 1.4%.

In annual terms, inflation in Kazakhstan stood at 9.3% in September 2026, compared with 9.8% in August 2026.

According to Trend calculations, the pace of disinflation picked up in September: annual inflation fell by 0.5 percentage points versus 0.4 points a month earlier (10.2% in July to 9.8% in August). With monthly price growth unchanged at 0.6%, the slowdown came entirely from a favorable base effect, not from weaker current price momentum.

Food was the main driver of the slowdown. Annual food inflation dropped by 1.0 percentage point, almost twice the August decline of 0.6 points. Food's contribution to the headline figure shrank by 0.4 points, from 3.6 to 3.2 points, while the contribution of the other categories stayed at 1 point. Food inflation has now fallen below that of paid services (8.5% vs 8.9%), whereas in August it was still 0.6 points higher. This is largely a cyclical, seasonal effect from the harvest and falling vegetable prices.

The underlying components are slowing much more weakly. Non-food inflation eased by only 0.4 points, comparable to August's 0.3 points. Paid services stalled at 8.9%, after easing by 0.3 points in August. As a result, the gap between non-food and food inflation widened from 1.9 to 2.5 points.

World.title: Iran exports $174M in goods through Qom Province customs
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 11. Iran exported around $174 million worth of goods weighing 136,000 tons through customs offices in the central Qom Province during the first six months of the current Iranian year (March 21–September 22, 2026).

According to the Qom Province Customs Administration, Director General Esfandiyar Derikvand said this.

"During the six-month period, goods were exported through the province’s customs offices to many countries, and the province is diversifying its foreign markets," he said.

Derikvand said the province’s customs offices play an important role in Qom’s economic development. Revenue from the province’s customs offices increased by 300% during the six months compared with the same period of the previous Iranian year, reaching 50 trillion rials (about $28.7 million).

Derikvand added that the Qom Province Customs Administration is focused on developing trade activities, particularly exports. In this regard, it is cooperating with local businesses to help them export their products to targeted markets as quickly as possible.

The customs official said the production of export-oriented goods by industrial enterprises in Qom Province is among the key priorities for promoting economic development and expanding employment opportunities. In recent years, businesses in the industrial sector have made significant efforts to achieve this strategic goal.

According to Trend’s analysis, the expansion of industrial activity in Qom Province is being carried out in line with indicators and priorities set by the province. Within this framework, priority is given to technology-oriented, knowledge-based, environmentally friendly, employment-generating and export-oriented industrial projects in terms of obtaining the necessary permits and receiving government support.

The province has 13 industrial parks and zones. More than 2,000 industrial enterprises operate in Qom’s industrial parks and zones, providing employment opportunities for more than 50,000 people and producing products needed by the country.

World.title: Prime Minister of Cambodia arrives in Azerbaijan for official visit
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 11. Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet arrived in the Republic of Azerbaijan on an official visit.

An honor guard was lined up at Heydar Aliyev International Airport, where the national flags of both countries were flying, in honor of the distinguished guest.

Prime Minister of Cambodia Hun Manet and his wife, Pich Chanmony, were welcomed by Azerbaijan’s Deputy Prime Minister Samir Sharifov, Deputy Foreign Minister Elnur Mammadov, and other officials.

World.title: Russia interfered in Brexit referendum, British PM says
World.content:
Russia clearly interfered in Britain's vote to leave the European Union, according to UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

In excerpts from The Rest is Politics podcast released Sunday, Mr Burnham said he asked his advisers after becoming prime minister in July whether Russia interfered in the 2016 referendum.

Investigations into the 2016 US elections suggested Russia sought to undermine Hilary Clinton's campaign and favour now-president Donald Trump.

"I asked the question coming to Downing Street, 'Was there interference in the 2016 referendum from Russia?'" he said.

"I've had the clear answer that yes, there was.

"These things are important now to put clearly on the record and I believe help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia."

Mr Burnham did not spell out how Russia interfered in the referendum and did not provide evidence.

More than 50 per cent of Britons voted to leave the EU. (Reuters: Henry Nicholls)

British voters elected to leave the EU in 2016, with 52 per cent voting for Brexit compared with 48 per cent.

However Mr Burnham last month said he could campaign to bring the UK back into the EU at the next general election.

Russia has long said it does not meddle in other countries' elections or referendums.

The Russian embassy in London did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

UK intelligence agencies have warned about the increasing threat of Russian interference in Britain's democratic institutions.

Mr Burnham's comments on the podcast are believed to be the first time a British prime minister has publicly acknowledged Russian interference in the Brexit vote.

The far-right Alternative for Germany (AFD) party has surged in popularity in recent years. ( Reuters: Christian Mang)

Mr Burnham said he spoke to German Chancellor Friedrich Merz about possible links between Russia and the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party when the two leaders met last week in Berlin.

"He was saying to me that the AfD are clearly linked to Russia, funded I believe," Mr Burnham said.

New UK PM Burnham meets Zelenskyy Downing Street said the meeting was designed to underscore Britain's steadfast support for Ukraine.

"There is certainly misinformation, disinformation that is emanating from Russia into German politics."

The UK parliament's Intelligence and Security Committee found in 2020 that the government failed to fully assess the impact Russian state-run media and "troll" accounts could have had on the EU referendum.

AP/Reuters

World.title: Cow 'Fitbit' helps pastoralists care for newborn calves
World.content:
When Kim Forrester started School of the Air at his family's station in Western Australia's remote Gascoyne, his only means of communication was a pedal radio.

Today he live streams water tank levels from his paddocks on his mobile phone and checks cattle data on his computer.

"Before was either on the motorbike or in the aeroplane or in a motor car and driving vast distances," Mr Forrester said.

"Now we've got a pretty good handle on it from an iPad."

Technology has helped make work at Winning Station more efficient and reliable. (Supplied: Lily Pillips)

Mr Forrester runs 10,000 head of cattle over more than 300,000 hectares at Winning Station, near Coral Bay, about 1,100 kilometres north of Perth.

His job is still driven by manual labour, but as Australia's agriculture industry rapidly digitises, he said embracing technology was critical.

Kim Forrester's family has been at Winning Station for decades. (ABC Rural: Lucie Bell)

"You're trying to operate with the least amount of labour you possibly can, purely to survive," he said.

"No doubt with AI coming along, the next 10 years will be an amazing development.

" Probably in 10 years we won't be using helicopters, we'll be sitting in shipping containers flying drones. "

Charbray cattle at Winning Station. (Supplied: Lily Pillips)

AgTech divide

The tech developments are helping tackle some of the biggest challenges in the agriculture industry.

While southern dairy farms were early adopters, challenges around distance and infrastructure made things more challenging across northern Australia.

The calf's ear tag measures behaviour and its GPS collar tracks movement. (Supplied: Dr Anita Chang)

Northern Territory Department of Agriculture and Fisheries (NTDAF) livestock team leader Christie Pearson said the scale of operations was vastly different.

"If you think about a standard property down south, you've probably got less than a couple of hundred head, or you've got animals that you can physically see in the paddock," Ms Pearson said.

"Up here we're still having contracting camps out, we're still mustering, we're still using helicopters.

" It's still very much the Wild West in a lot of ways. "

'Fitbits' help track losses

At Manbulloo Station just outside Katherine, Ms Pearson observes the movements of 140 cows wearing technology similar to the Fitbit activity monitors used to track exercise in humans.

She is collecting data on maternal behaviours and herd interactions to better understand calf loss.

A calf feeding at Belmont Station in Rockhampton. (Supplied: Dr Anita Chang)

The herd is sporting ear tags and GPS collars that track movement and behaviours, including time spent ruminating and grazing, herd interactions, and cows' responses to calf loss.

Ms Pearson said they had noticed each cow's maternal behaviours were different.

"There's some cows that leave their calves out in the paddock, and they walk into water for up to a week after calving before they'll bring their calf into the water," she said.

"Then there's some calves who are born right near the water."

These tracking device trials are taking place across two northern pastoral properties as part of Central Queensland (CQ) University's "Mooternal" project.

Anita Chang is using Fitbit-style devices to monitor maternal behaviour in cows. (ABC Rural: Jessica D'Souza )

Senior researcher Anita Chang has been monitoring 100 cows at Belmont Station in Rockhampton for more than a year, with surprising results.

"Last year at Belmont we found that one calf was cross-suckling with two separate cows, so there were two cows that were equally invested in the calf's survival," Dr Chang said.

"In some instances it's as much about the calf as it is about the cow, so the calf is the one pursuing different nursing opportunities."

The trials will continue for a further three years.

Back on Winning Station, Kim Forrester believes easy access to technology could be game-changing.

"Surviving calves on the ground is our biggest profit driver," Mr Forrester said.

"One death of a calf means that cow hasn't produced a calf that year, so you're running that cow, but no income off it."

World.title: Trees down, hail fell across Adelaide during storm
World.content:
Damaging winds and hailstones have caused damage across Adelaide overnight, with trees blocking roads and falling onto vehicles.

More than 100 calls for help were received by the State Emergency Service since Sunday afternoon, with 80 per cent of reports due to fallen trees.

Vale Park resident Niall Dowdell had returned home after a trip to the Barossa to celebrate his wedding anniversary when the storm blew through.

"It just came through pretty rapidly," he said.

Niall Dowdell's car was struck by a falling tree. (ABC News: Olivia Mason)

When he went outside to move his car to safety, he was greeted by a large tree that had fallen onto the front of his car.

"We heard a bit of thunder and then the rain just came in really heavy and then within a couple of minutes I've come out and the tree's down on my car," Mr Dowdell said.

"I think maybe a lightning strike's hit the tree."

A Nailsworth resident emerged to find a neighbour's trampoline had blown into their yard. (Supplied)

Several storms crossed South Australia and metropolitan Adelaide on Sunday afternoon, mostly clearing by 9pm.

The SES reported 3 centimetres of hailstones fell at Happy Valley at 7:45 pm yesterday.

Large hailstones fell across Adelaide. (Supplied: Sharon O'Grady)

SES duty officer Ian Bonython said the majority of its call-outs were in Adelaide's north, and had largely ended by the night.

Multiple reports of fallen trees occurred across Adelaide's inner north-east from Payneham towards Paradise yesterday.

Most of the fallen trees were reported in Adelaide's north-eastern suburbs. (ABC News)

The Bureau of Meteorology said storm activity would continue across South Australia on Monday.

"Still seeing a lot of cloud, showers and certainly still some rumbles of thunder but we will continue to see it contract into north-eastern parts of the state today," said Urshla Connor, senior forecaster at the Bureau of Meteorology.

World.title: Neighbours describe explosions as Melbourne tobacco shop burns down
World.content:
Police are investigating a suspicious fire that gutted a tobacco store in Fitzroy North and woke residents with loud explosions.

Emergency services were called to reports of explosions on St Georges Road about 3:45am and arrived to find the shop completely engulfed in flames.

Residents say the sound of explosions could be heard as the fire burned this morning. (ABC News: Costa Haritos)

Firefighters attempted to stop the fire spreading to neighbouring properties, with two other businesses also damaged.

No one was inside the tobacco store, which was completely destroyed by the fire.

One nearby resident said she and her partner heard and smelled the fire before seeing it, after being woken in the middle of the night.

"It sounded like sparks going off in different areas of the neighbourhood, and then two minutes later, just a massive explosion," she said.

"We went outside our front door and it was big, black smoke coming across."

Firefighters worked to extinguish the blaze, but were unable to prevent two neighbouring businesses being damaged by the fire. (ABC News: Costa Haritos)

A crime scene has been established, and investigators believe one or multiple offenders broke into the shop and set it alight.

A dark-coloured vehicle was seen leaving the scene by witnesses.

Anyone who witnessed the incident, has dashcam or CCTV footage or anyone with information is urged to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000 or submit a confidential report online.

The Fitzroy North fire is the latest in a string of suspicious fires being investigated by police.

Last week, Victoria Police said a targeted operation was working to drive down arsons across the state and had made more than 160 arrests this year.

World.title: Environmental watchdog to review new Kimberley gas project
World.content:
The company behind a proposed gas project in Western Australia's Kimberley says it could meet the region's power demands with locally produced energy for the first time.

Buru Energy referred its Rafael conventional gas project to WA's Environmental Protection Authority (EPA) for review in early October.

The proposal involves developing a facility at the project site, located in the Kimberley's Canning Basin about 85 kilometres south of Derby, to process conventional gas from two co-located production wells.

Conventional gas is natural gas extracted using simple drilling and pumping methods, as opposed to unconventional extraction methods like hydraulic fracturing, or fracking.

Well testing underway at Buru Energy's Rafael conventional gas project. (Supplied: Buru Energy)

Buru executive chairman David Maxwell said the Rafael project was the only proven conventional gas and liquids resource in the greater Kimberley region.

"At the moment, the Kimberley relies on imported energy … from Karratha, Perth, Darwin, and Asia," he said.

" It's the first opportunity for the Kimberley to have gas and LPG [Liquefied Petroleum Gas] in particular, supplied from within the region. "

He said the Rafael project would improve energy security and be cost-effective, with reduced road traffic another potential benefit.

Up to 300 tonnes of Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) would be produced at the Rafael plant per day — the equivalent of about 16 or 17 terajoules of energy — alongside LPG and condensate.

Mr Maxwell said the Kimberley used between six and 13 terajoules per day for power generation, with the amount varying based on the time of year.

"We have the capacity to supply 100 per cent of the Kimberley's gas demand," he said.

"We'll also supply beyond the Kimberley into, for example, the northern Pilbara.

"In the case of LPG, we would be supplying in the order of a quarter to a third of the Kimberley's LPG demand."

Concerns over fracking

The West Australian government has banned fracking in over 98 per cent of the state, but this does not include parts of the Kimberley including the Canning Basin.

Earlier this year, WA's EPA recommended a fracking proposal by Black Mountain Energy subsidiary Bennett Resources go ahead subject to conditions.

The Valhalla Gas Exploration and Appraisal Program would see up to 20 exploration and appraisal wells drilled in the basin.

A record 8,000 appeals were lodged against the project.

Community members gather in Broome to protest the Valhalla fracking proposal. (ABC Kimberley: Dunja Karagic )

When asked about the fracking proposal in Broome this month, WA Mines Minister Daniel Pastorelli said the method had drawn varied perspectives.

"I understand everyone has differing views on these types of things and I respect that completely," he said.

"Obviously our policy and our approach is based on science, and that is what we're doing when it comes to hydraulic fracturing."

Daniel Pastorelli acknowledges fracking is a controversial topic. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Environmentalists have expressed concern Buru's Rafael project, although a conventional gas project, could pave the way for fracking to occur in the future.

Environs Kimberley executive director Martin Pritchard said Rafael "could be a Trojan horse for fracking".

"They (Buru) might be saying right now that they're not intending on fracking, but their statements to the ASX clearly say that they want to undertake fracking in the future," he said.

Buru's David Maxwell rejected the accusation.

"It's got nothing to do with fracking at all," he said.

"And if there was any fracking involved — and I stress there is not — that would be a separate [EPA] referral, a separate application and a separate approval process and we're not in that process at all."

Buru Energy's Yulleroo 2 wellhead 60 kilometres east of Broome was fracked in 2010. (ABC Kimberley: Ben Collins)

The company previously used the hydraulic fracturing technique at its Yulleroo gas field also in the Canning Basin, but Mr Maxwell said it no longer did so.

"We do not currently practice hydraulic fracturing," he said.

"In the past Buru has, but Buru has put that on the shelf, and at the moment we have no plans for fracture stimulation."

Mr Pritchard said solar and batteries, rather than gas fields, were the way forward for cheaper and cleaner electricity in the Kimberley.

"What we need to be doing is ramping up renewable energy, and we need to do that as quickly as possible," Mr Pritchard said.

Mr Maxwell said Buru expected a decision from the EPA by the end of the year and hoped to produce the first gas by early 2029.

World.title: Live: Roos and Swans in Blakey standoff, Suns and Hawks complete double-deal
World.content:
(Getty Images)

I suspected this might be the case when the megadeal went through on Friday, but it was confirmed in various reporting over the weekend. Port Adelaide is looking to trade out pick five in this year's draft to the highest bidder, safe in the knowledge it already has a healthy suite of picks after its previous dealings.

So who do they trade it to? It depends what they want. All of Richmond, West Coast, Carlton and Essendon are said to be in the race.

If they want future picks — and they very much do, as they will have at least two, or possibly three, highly rated players to match bids on in the 2027 draft — then they will be talking to Richmond and West Coast.

If they want picks this year — and they may well do, as it is a deep draft and the last pre-Tassie — then Carlton and Essendon have a better chance of turning their heads.

Reading between the lines, it seems Richmond is the current frontrunner. Having two top-five picks in this draft would be a coup for the Tigers. You could say the same for West Coast, but would the Eagles be willing to go above and beyond to secure the pick?

The bad news is there is no guarantee this trade gets done by Wednesday night, as there is another window over the next couple of weeks in which draft picks can be exchanged.

World.title: Netanyahu demands probe into soldiers' involvement in Gaza documentary
World.content:
Israel's prime minister is demanding a sweeping investigation and prosecution of any soldiers who took part in an explosive documentary about his country's conduct in Gaza.

NAZA, which details how Israel's military has waged a deadly campaign in the war-ravaged strip, was released to critical acclaim at the Venice International Film Festival last month.

Testimony from soldiers accused the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) of systematic mass civilian killings.

It fuelled fierce debate in Israel and the filmmakers behind the documentary, Oscar-winning Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, faced allegations of treason and threats against them and their families.

Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor have not yet returned home to Israel, where their film has been fiercely criticised. (Supplied: Committee to Protect Journalists)

Benjamin Netanyahu has now written to the heads of the IDF, domestic intelligence agency Shin Bet and the country's attorney-general — who has the power to order prosecutions — to investigate any soldiers who took part in NAZA.

"The film spins a false, misleading, and biased narrative that slanders the State of Israel and the IDF globally and severely damages Israel's standing," Mr Netanyahu wrote.

He said those involved should face prosecution for leaking sensitive information, criminal libel and damaging Israel's diplomatic and security interests.

Mr Netanyahu and senior members of his ministry had already promised to pursue legislation giving the government the power to strip citizenship from people who smeared Israeli soldiers.

Israeli doco makers accused of 'treason' in Israel NAZA, by Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, accuses the Israeli army of systematic mass civilian killings in Gaza.

NAZA, which is a reference to an Israeli military acronym referring to collateral damage, includes interviews with two dozen soldiers and intelligence officials, speaking on the condition of anonymity.

Their testimony paints a vivid and disturbing picture of the techniques used by the IDF in Gaza, including artificial intelligence, to assess targets.

The IDF has rejected the film's allegations, and the Israeli government has released a counter-documentary to try to discredit it.

Various organisations, including Reporters Without Borders, had condemned the Netanyahu government's attacks on NAZA and its team, arguing it was an example of attacks against the media ahead of the Israeli election on October 27.

One of Mr Netanyahu's challengers in the polls, Gadi Eisenkot, has echoed the government's criticism of the film.

NAZA is scheduled to start screening in some Australian cinemas later this week.

The filmmakers won an Academy Award for their 2024 film No Other Land, which exposed the violent behaviour of Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank and the support they received from the IDF.

World.title: Man killed in car crash in Victoria's Mallee region
World.content:
A 43-year-old man has been killed in a crash at Watchem West, about 300 kilometres north-west of Melbourne.

Police said the driver lost control on Watchem-Warracknabeal Road, in Victoria's Mallee region, and crashed into trees at 4pm yesterday.

Detectives from the Major Collision Investigation Unit are investigating the incident.

The provisional 2026 Victorian road toll now stands at 202.

Anyone with information is urged to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000, or report anonymously to www.crimestoppersvic.com.au.

The Australian sharemarket has started the week in positive territory while oil markets edged higher as renewed strikes on Saudi Arabia’s main airport and a fresh tanker attack near the Strait of Hormuz raised the prospect that intensifying hostilities could exacerbate supply risks. The S&P/ ASX 200 was up 26.1 points, or 0.3 per cent, in early trade to 8742.7. The Australian dollar was trading at US69.78¢. Wall Street closed a positive week with more gains. AP Brent crude was near $US105 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate traded around $US92. King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh came under attack again overnight by Iran-backed Houthi militants, a day after a strike killed 12 people. Major Middle Eastern oil producers have managed to resume crude exports through Hormuz close to pre-conflict levels, but the spike in tanker attacks and heightened tensions across the region could threaten those flows. On Friday, the S&P 500 climbed 0.6 per cent for its first gain since setting its all-time high three days earlier. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 423 points, or 0.8 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite rose 0.6 per cent.



Trump announced on Sunday (US time) that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an “energy ceasefire” effective immediately. “Both parties have agreed. BusinessWorkplaceWorkplace culture McKinsey strips Australian partner of leadership role after ‘glass ceiling’ comments Colin Kruger Updated October 12, 2026 — 9:52am ,first published 8:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Global consulting giant McKinsey & Co had dumped senior Australian partner Chris Bradley from his leadership role at the firm’s research arm after he posted online comments questioning the uphill battle female executives face in the workplace. The firm confirmed that he had been removed from his board role at the McKinsey Global Institute, its high-profile business and economic research unit. Bradley – a member of Sydney-based conservative think tank, The Centre for Independent Studies – remains a senior partner at the firm. McKinsey partner Chris Bradley called the glass cliff “a very convenient way to always be a victim in the rain” in the deleted posts and generally questioned whether the concept even existed. Peter Rae The decision came after an internal review sparked by Bradley’s LinkedIn back-and-forth last month with one of the authors of a new book that discusses the workplace “glass cliff” for women. The comments were deleted and McKinsey previously distanced itself from Bradley’s remarks. “Following our conduct review process, we have removed the partner from his leadership roles, including at the McKinsey Global Institute. His public comments fell well short of the standards we expect at our firm,” McKinsey spokesman Taylor Burns said. Bradley also served as a leader on some internal committees, Burns said.



Bradley couldn’t be reached immediately for comment outside normal business hours. Related Article Gender equality Informed of a job interview at 4am, but female garbo’s discrimination claim still fails The term glass cliff was coined by academics to describe the phenomenon in which female leaders are more likely to be offered chief executive officer jobs at struggling companies. Proponents of the theory say research shows that women are more likely to get an opportunity to be CEO when a company is in crisis or turnaround mode. Bradley called the glass cliff “a very convenient way to always be a victim in the rain” in the deleted posts and generally questioned whether the concept even existed. McKinsey has long sought to advance the conversation about challenges women face in the workplace. The company has published a “Women in the Workplace” study, compiled with Sheryl Sandberg’s Lean In advocacy group, for more than a decade.



Bradley is the author of A Century of Plenty and the father of three daughters, according to his McKinsey profile. A 2020 report from McKinsey about women working in healthcare references the term “glass cliff” when outlining hurdles cited by women of colour. ‘Following our conduct review process, we have removed the partner from his leadership roles, including at the McKinsey Global Institute. His public comments fell well short of the standards we expect at our firm.’ McKinsey spokesperson Taylor Burns Bradley also wrote in the recent LinkedIn exchange that “we once had a problem of female advancement to CEO, but now we have a new problem that the jobs they get are too hard? Is this actually a thing?” Julia Carreon, a former Wall Street executive and co-author of the book Walking on Broken Glass: Navigating the Aftermath of the Glass Ceiling, commented on Bradley’s LinkedIn post, saying: “Aren’t people from McKinsey & Company supposed to know these things?



“I understand you ARE the establishment, but this is surprising.” Related Article Mentoring How ‘reverse mentoring’ is being used by unexpected high-flyers at work In response to Carreon, Bradley said: “I am not going to start researching glass cliffs as I don’t think it ranks in the top 1000 problems of the world.” Carreon accused Bradley of displaying “willful ignorance” and said she hoped this was a “teaching moment for Mr Bradley and McKinsey”. In a LinkedIn post on Monday morning she said his comments “showcases exactly what Shannon Nutter and I hoped to expose in our new book Walking on Broken Glass: the absurd amount of energy women are forced to spend proving our own experiences are real.”

World.title: ‘Do not break it’: Ukraine backs ‘energy ceasefire’ after Trump declares surprise deal is done
World.content:
Updated WorldEuropeRussia-Ukraine war ‘Do not break it’: Ukraine backs ‘energy ceasefire’ after Trump declares surprise deal is done David Crowe Updated October 12, 2026 — 8:56am ,first published 3:36am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. London: Ukraine has signalled it is willing to accept an energy ceasefire with Russia after US President Donald Trump announced the surprise move and claimed both sides of the war would back the plan with immediate effect. But the White House announcement was followed within hours by Russian strikes on a power plant in eastern Ukraine and other targets, while there was silence from the Kremlin on whether it would agree to a truce. US President Donald Trump walks on the South Lawn of the White House on Saturday evening. Bloomberg Amid confusion over Trump’s claims, reports spread that the US president was threatening to cut supplies of weapons to Ukraine under a major program funded by European nations, using this as leverage to force Ukraine to stop striking oil refineries in Russia. Trump took Ukrainian leaders by surprise with a declaration on social media that the energy ceasefire would go ahead, amid fierce criticism of his deal to ease trade bans on Russia so it could export diesel fuel to American customers.



His move was backed within an hour by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on the condition that Russian President Vladimir Putin was also willing to stop the duelling attacks on energy assets. “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine,” Trump declared on Sunday in Washington DC (early Monday morning AEST). View post on X “Both parties have agreed. Do not break it! Thank you for your attention to this matter.” Ukrainian official told media in Kyiv that they had no information about an energy ceasefire, spreading confusion over the terms of any negotiation and whether Trump had leapt ahead of negotiations to claim an outcome that did not exist.



Zelensky responded to the news soon afterwards by telling US media outlet Axios that he was ready to support a deal to stop the attacks. Related Article Updated

Russia-Ukraine war ‘Time for a new president’: Trump calls on Zelensky to go amid diesel stoush “The ceasefire announcement was news for me,” Zelensky told Axios reporter Barack Ravid, who reported the comments on X. “But if Russians agree to an energy ceasefire Ukraine will agree. If president Trump negotiated it with Putin – please tell us when the ceasefire begins – we are ready and we will accept it” Zelensky held a quick succession of phone calls with NATO leaders in the hours after Trump’s statement, drawing public support from French President Emmanuel Macron and others who backed the idea of an energy truce but emphasised that Russia was to blame for its intensifying attacks.



Britain also backed Trump’s call for a sustained energy ceasefire, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in a post on X. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she “fully supported” Zelensky’s call for a ceasefire that would protect energy infrastructure as well as global food supplies. View post on X Von der Leyen, who spoke to Zelensky on Sunday, said European Union leaders would meet this week to discuss funding for Ukraine including money for drones and missiles. Zelensky said he had spoken to Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte. “We are awaiting details from the American side,” he said in a post on X.



Hours later, with no response from Putin on Trump’s claimed ceasefire, the Ukrainian leader said there was no change in the Russian attacks. Related Article Trump's White House Trump strikes deal with Putin for Russian diesel “There have been glide bomb strikes and strikes on our energy infrastructure too,” Zelensky said on Sunday night (about 5am on Monday, AEDT). “A power plant in Kharkiv was attacked this evening. Overall, this past week alone, the Russians have carried out more than 200 strikes on our electricity generation and transmission facilities in Ukraine, and another 17 strikes this week targeted gas and oil facilities. They have killed more than 150 of our people, and more than 700 people have been wounded.” Russia has intensified its attacks on civilian targets in Ukraine using ballistic missiles as well as jet-powered drones that are significantly faster than propeller-based drones and evade air defences, heightening concerns in Kyiv about a shortage of interceptor drones and missiles to shield potential targets.



Zelensky has responded with more powerful attacks on Russian supply lines and infrastructure, including oil refineries, contributing to a shortage of fuel in parts of Russia and greater challenges for oil companies exporting diesel to world markets. In a phone call on September 21, Trump urged Zelensky to stop the attacks on oil refineries because they were driving up the cost of diesel on world markets. While the two leaders met in New York that week on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, there was no change to the Ukrainian strategy. Trump stung the Ukrainian leadership on Friday by announcing the diesel agreement with Russia, triggering criticism that he had handed a significant victory to Putin by allowing Russia to generate more export revenue from oil regardless of years of Western attempts to limit its trade. Trump aired his frustration on Saturday by saying Ukraine should hold elections to replace Zelensky. “It’s time for Ukraine to get a new president,” he told reporters. He added that he had told the Ukrainian president not to hit refineries. “He better damn well stop,” Trump said.



The Financial Times reported that the US was threatening to stop the weapons mechanism known as PURL, the Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List, under which European and other nations fund the supply of equipment from American companies to Ukraine. Australia made a $100 million pledge to PURL in June, adding to an earlier $50 million payment. Officials told the Financial Times that the US was lobbying European leaders to urge Kyiv to stop the attacks on Russian oil refineries. On Sunday, Zelensky told US broadcaster ABC that he could prepare a plan for a new presidential election if the US president could arrange a two-month ceasefire with Putin.
