Australian rock band Powderfinger have confirmed their national tour dates just days after announcing their reunion – and 16 years after breaking up. The 18-stadium show tour includes dates in Sydney, Melbourne, Cairns, Perth, and Adelaide and kicks off in the band’s hometown, Brisbane. Australian rock band Powderfinger have confirmed their national tour dates. Giulia Giannini McGauran Described on the band’s website as a “travelling rock’n’roll circus”, Powderfinger said the shows would be “part festival, part spectacle and set to be filled with the communal joy of thousands of fans, gathering offline to experience the music they love, together”. “We are absolutely ecstatic to be coming together to play again,” the band said in a statement posted to a new website on Monday morning. “Over the years there have been tons of suggestions for us to go back on the road but, until now, it never felt quite right or lined up for all of us.”



The band will curate an all-Australian line-up of support acts – with different artists joining in each city – and the tour is partnering with homeless charity Mission Australia. The tour dates are: Friday September 3 – Brisbane Showgrounds, Brisbane

Saturday September 4 – Brisbane Showgrounds, Brisbane

Friday September 10 – Brisbane Showgrounds, Brisbane

Saturday September 11 – Brisbane Showgrounds, Brisbane

Friday September 17 – Cazalys Stadium, Cairns

Saturday September 18 – Cazalys Stadium, Cairns

Friday September 24 – Wellington Square, Perth

Saturday September 25 – Wellington Square, Perth

Friday October 1 – The Domain, Sydney

Saturday October 2 – The Domain, Sydney

Friday October 8 – The Domain, Sydney

Saturday October 9 – The Domain, Sydney

Friday October 15 – Ellis Park, Adelaide

Saturday October 16 – Ellis Park, Adelaide

Friday October 22 – Melbourne Park Oval, Melbourne

Saturday October 23 – Melbourne Park Oval, Melbourne

Friday October 29 – Melbourne Park Oval, Melbourne

Saturday October 30 – Melbourne Park Oval, Melbourne Powderfinger tickets will go on presale on October 14 on Ticketmaster. Public sale will begin October 19, and all cities’ sale times are subject to their time zones. On Friday, the band uploaded videos to various social media platforms to confirm their reunion and announce a national tour after much speculation. “Hello, everyone. We’re Powderfinger, and we’ve got a little announcement to make for you today,” guitarist and vocalist Bernard “Bernie” Fanning said in the YouTube video.



“We always said that if we were going to get back together to do some shows, that you guys would be the first to know. And so now you’re the first to know. We’re going to do some shows all around Australia from September next year.” In the days leading up to the announcement, displays in Brisbane, Melbourne and Sydney featured sprawling letters, symbols and numbers connected to an Instagram account called The Return of the Electric Horsemen. Fans speculated it referenced Powderfinger’s song (Return of) The Electric Horseman from their 1996 album Double Allergic. Later, the band’s official Instagram posted the same image. Powderfinger. The band last performed at an impromptu reunion during Splendour in the Grass in 2017.



Fans perched above the Amphitheatre leapt to their feet and screamed with approval as Fanning’s former bandmates – Darren “Darius” Middleton, Ian “Hoggy” Haug and John “JC” Collins – readied their instruments. Drummer Jonathon “Cogsy” Coghill was the only absent member. Related Article Opinion

Australian music These days turned out nothing like I’d planned. Powderfinger just made sure of it Chris Paine National Content Director In the note to fans on their website, Powderfinger said support from both new and long-term fans had prompted the new tour. “It feels right to bring all of these people – including our kids who were too young to see us play – together for a special run of shows around the country next year,” the statement said. “People often tell us that our music is connected to their most treasured and joyous memories. We hope to spread a little more of that joy when we make our way around the country with some of Australia’s best established and upcoming talent, and to make some new memories for us all.“



The Queensland government took credit on Monday morning for securing back-to-back shows in the regional centre of Cairns, describing the concerts as a win for local businesses. “Powderfinger are Queensland legends, a Queensland story, so it’s only fitting that Queensland has secured this major coup,” Premier David Crisafulli said. “We went after this because we knew how much this would mean to Queenslanders, especially those in regional areas … Queensland has a plan to become the events capital of the country.” The state has repeatedly missed out on major touring acts, including Oasis, Taylor Swift and Coldplay.



Powderfinger formed in Brisbane in 1989 after Haug, an aspiring rock star who had played in pubs illegally as a teenager, created the band with two other high school friends, including Collins. Not long after, the five-piece as we know them today formed under a name inspired by a Neil Young song. In 1992, the band recorded their self-titled debut EP Powderfinger, also called The Blue. A second EP, Transfusion soon followed and in 1994 released debut album Parable for Wooden Ears. However, their 1996 release Double Allergic made them stars and they were soon touring worldwide, topping Triple J and ARIA charts, as well as booking big festival slots, including all dates for the Big Day Out. In total, Powderfinger have released seven studio albums, including anthems such as My Happiness, These Days, Sunsets, On My Mind, Burn Your Name and Pick You Up. Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson says Australia should not be promoting violence, but will have trouble blocking the livestreaming of a US execution from being streamed in Australia.

“My basic principle is we shouldn’t be promoting that sort of violence, and so my fundamental view is yes, I think it’s enormously problematic to tolerate this type of behaviour,” he told ABC Radio National earlier when asked whether the government should block it.

“But the challenge is going to be how do you do that in a way that doesn’t amount to a censorship ban on the internet? How are you going to do that without creating the artifice to be able to block content on the internet and create an online portal of censorship?”

The execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring dozens more in a shooting at the Fort Hood military base in 2009, will be the first by military firing squad since World War II. The execution was approved by US President Donald Trump last week on the recommendation of Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth who originally said it would be a public event.

World.content:
NationalVictoriaCrime ‘Knocked me over’: Safety fears at Melbourne marathon as teen charged with hitting woman Alexander Darling and Shelby Brooks October 12, 2026 — 6:48am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. A teen boy has been charged with a string of offences after allegedly hitting a woman with a stolen car as tens of thousands of people were running in the Melbourne Marathon nearby. It comes as runners complained of safety concerns during the marathon, including one who claimed he and others were struck by pacing vehicles. The teenager was arrested late morning Sunday after allegedly driving a stolen car through the CBD. Nine News Police drew their guns on the teen’s Ford Escape after it hit the 57-year-old at the corner of Flinders and Elizabeth streets around 10.30am, about 150 metres from where tens of thousands of runners were taking part in the Melbourne marathon. The SUV went on to hit several parked cars and street signs on Flinders Lane. The boy was eventually arrested without incident at Albert Park. Overnight, police charged him with ten offences, including reckless conduct endangering serious injury and failing to render assistance. The latter offence carries a penalty of up to ten years in prison on its own.



Related Article Melbourne Marathon This athletics great says the Melbourne Marathon track was the ‘best ever’ Around the same time, two competitors were reportedly injured by course vehicles in the Albert Park area. Dr Nathan Freeman, based in Tasmania, took to social media claiming that he came across a female runner who had been hit by the pacer car for the men’s half-marathon, though she herself was running in the marathon. Freeman said when he stopped to offer assistance, a passing motorcycle also there for the event clipped his back. “It actually knocked me over almost down onto the patient,” he said. “And they didn’t even stop, they just continued on.”



Freeman said the other runner would need surgery for a “major injury”, and weeks of recovery. “It’s good that they’ll be fine but just not acceptable [that this has happened],” he said. Another witness, Mark, told 3AW he saw a runner get hit at Albert Park. He said he was in the last six kilometres of the marathon when bikes pacing the half-marathon leaders passed him. “The bikes sped past with their horns on, but then the cars just ploughed, and there wasn’t enough room for the slower marathon runners and the fast pace car, and the pace car just hit one of the marathon runners.” It wasn’t immediately clear whether this was the same accident Freeman witnessed before stopping to help.



The Age has contacted the Melbourne Marathon and Ambulance Victoria for comment. Police allege the vehicle that hit the woman on Flinders Street was stolen from a business in Cranbourne South, nearly an hour’s drive from Melbourne, at 2am on Sunday. The teen has been held in custody overnight ahead of facing children’s court on Monday morning, while police have confirmed the incident was not an act of terrorism or a targeted attack. The woman suffered injuries to her upper body, though authorities say these are not life-threatening, and she remains in hospital as of the most recent update. The incident ultimately had no impact on the race, which was won by legendary marathon runner Eliud Kipchoge in a record time. Be the first to know when major news happens.

Bradley – a member of Sydney-based conservative think tank, The Centre for Independent Studies – remains a senior partner at the firm. McKinsey partner Chris Bradley called the glass cliff “a very convenient way to always be a victim in the rain” in the deleted posts and generally questioned whether the concept even existed. Peter Rae The decision came after an internal review sparked by Bradley’s LinkedIn back-and-forth last month with one of the authors of a new book that discusses the workplace “glass cliff” for women. The comments were deleted and McKinsey previously distanced itself from Bradley’s remarks. “Following our conduct review process, we have removed the partner from his leadership roles, including at the McKinsey Global Institute. His public comments fell well short of the standards we expect at our firm,” McKinsey spokesman Taylor Burns said. Bradley also served as a leader on some internal committees, Burns said.



Bradley couldn’t be reached immediately for comment outside normal business hours. Related Article Gender equality Informed of a job interview at 4am, but female garbo’s discrimination claim still fails The term glass cliff was coined by academics to describe the phenomenon in which female leaders are more likely to be offered chief executive officer jobs at struggling companies. Proponents of the theory say research shows that women are more likely to get an opportunity to be CEO when a company is in crisis or turnaround mode. Bradley called the glass cliff “a very convenient way to always be a victim in the rain” in the deleted posts and generally questioned whether the concept even existed. McKinsey has long sought to advance the conversation about challenges women face in the workplace. The company has published a “Women in the Workplace” study, compiled with Sheryl Sandberg’s Lean In advocacy group, for more than a decade.



Bradley is the author of A Century of Plenty and the father of three daughters, according to his McKinsey profile. A 2020 report from McKinsey about women working in healthcare references the term “glass cliff” when outlining hurdles cited by women of colour. ‘Following our conduct review process, we have removed the partner from his leadership roles, including at the McKinsey Global Institute. His public comments fell well short of the standards we expect at our firm.’ McKinsey spokesperson Taylor Burns Bradley also wrote in the recent LinkedIn exchange that “we once had a problem of female advancement to CEO, but now we have a new problem that the jobs they get are too hard? Is this actually a thing?” Julia Carreon, a former Wall Street executive and co-author of the book Walking on Broken Glass: Navigating the Aftermath of the Glass Ceiling, commented on Bradley’s LinkedIn post, saying: “Aren’t people from McKinsey & Company supposed to know these things?



“I understand you ARE the establishment, but this is surprising.” Related Article Mentoring How ‘reverse mentoring’ is being used by unexpected high-flyers at work In response to Carreon, Bradley said: “I am not going to start researching glass cliffs as I don’t think it ranks in the top 1000 problems of the world.” Carreon accused Bradley of displaying “willful ignorance” and said she hoped this was a “teaching moment for Mr Bradley and McKinsey”. In a LinkedIn post on Monday morning she said his comments “showcases exactly what Shannon Nutter and I hoped to expose in our new book Walking on Broken Glass: the absurd amount of energy women are forced to spend proving our own experiences are real.”

World.title: ‘Do not break it’: Ukraine backs ‘energy ceasefire’ after Trump declares surprise deal is done
World.content:
Updated WorldEuropeRussia-Ukraine war ‘Do not break it’: Ukraine backs ‘energy ceasefire’ after Trump declares surprise deal is done David Crowe Updated October 12, 2026 — 8:56am ,first published 3:36am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

London: Ukraine has signalled it is willing to accept an energy ceasefire with Russia after US President Donald Trump announced the surprise move and claimed both sides of the war would back the plan with immediate effect. But the White House announcement was followed within hours by Russian strikes on a power plant in eastern Ukraine and other targets, while there was silence from the Kremlin on whether it would agree to a truce. US President Donald Trump walks on the South Lawn of the White House on Saturday evening. Bloomberg Amid confusion over Trump’s claims, reports spread that the US president was threatening to cut supplies of weapons to Ukraine under a major program funded by European nations, using this as leverage to force Ukraine to stop striking oil refineries in Russia. Trump took Ukrainian leaders by surprise with a declaration on social media that the energy ceasefire would go ahead, amid fierce criticism of his deal to ease trade bans on Russia so it could export diesel fuel to American customers.



His move was backed within an hour by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on the condition that Russian President Vladimir Putin was also willing to stop the duelling attacks on energy assets. “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine,” Trump declared on Sunday in Washington DC (early Monday morning AEST). View post on X “Both parties have agreed. Do not break it! Thank you for your attention to this matter.” Ukrainian official told media in Kyiv that they had no information about an energy ceasefire, spreading confusion over the terms of any negotiation and whether Trump had leapt ahead of negotiations to claim an outcome that did not exist.



Zelensky responded to the news soon afterwards by telling US media outlet Axios that he was ready to support a deal to stop the attacks. Related Article Updated

Russia-Ukraine war ‘Time for a new president’: Trump calls on Zelensky to go amid diesel stoush “The ceasefire announcement was news for me,” Zelensky told Axios reporter Barack Ravid, who reported the comments on X. “But if Russians agree to an energy ceasefire Ukraine will agree. If president Trump negotiated it with Putin – please tell us when the ceasefire begins – we are ready and we will accept it” Zelensky held a quick succession of phone calls with NATO leaders in the hours after Trump’s statement, drawing public support from French President Emmanuel Macron and others who backed the idea of an energy truce but emphasised that Russia was to blame for its intensifying attacks.



Britain also backed Trump’s call for a sustained energy ceasefire, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in a post on X. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she “fully supported” Zelensky’s call for a ceasefire that would protect energy infrastructure as well as global food supplies. View post on X Von der Leyen, who spoke to Zelensky on Sunday, said European Union leaders would meet this week to discuss funding for Ukraine including money for drones and missiles. Zelensky said he had spoken to Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte. “We are awaiting details from the American side,” he said in a post on X.



Hours later, with no response from Putin on Trump’s claimed ceasefire, the Ukrainian leader said there was no change in the Russian attacks. Related Article Trump's White House Trump strikes deal with Putin for Russian diesel “There have been glide bomb strikes and strikes on our energy infrastructure too,” Zelensky said on Sunday night (about 5am on Monday, AEDT). “A power plant in Kharkiv was attacked this evening. Overall, this past week alone, the Russians have carried out more than 200 strikes on our electricity generation and transmission facilities in Ukraine, and another 17 strikes this week targeted gas and oil facilities. They have killed more than 150 of our people, and more than 700 people have been wounded.” Russia has intensified its attacks on civilian targets in Ukraine using ballistic missiles as well as jet-powered drones that are significantly faster than propeller-based drones and evade air defences, heightening concerns in Kyiv about a shortage of interceptor drones and missiles to shield potential targets.



Zelensky has responded with more powerful attacks on Russian supply lines and infrastructure, including oil refineries, contributing to a shortage of fuel in parts of Russia and greater challenges for oil companies exporting diesel to world markets. In a phone call on September 21, Trump urged Zelensky to stop the attacks on oil refineries because they were driving up the cost of diesel on world markets. While the two leaders met in New York that week on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, there was no change to the Ukrainian strategy. Trump stung the Ukrainian leadership on Friday by announcing the diesel agreement with Russia, triggering criticism that he had handed a significant victory to Putin by allowing Russia to generate more export revenue from oil regardless of years of Western attempts to limit its trade. Trump aired his frustration on Saturday by saying Ukraine should hold elections to replace Zelensky. “It’s time for Ukraine to get a new president,” he told reporters. He added that he had told the Ukrainian president not to hit refineries. “He better damn well stop,” Trump said.



The Financial Times reported that the US was threatening to stop the weapons mechanism known as PURL, the Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List, under which European and other nations fund the supply of equipment from American companies to Ukraine. Australia made a $100 million pledge to PURL in June, adding to an earlier $50 million payment. Officials told the Financial Times that the US was lobbying European leaders to urge Kyiv to stop the attacks on Russian oil refineries. On Sunday, Zelensky told US broadcaster ABC that he could prepare a plan for a new presidential election if the US president could arrange a two-month ceasefire with Putin. World.title: Fertile feral cats the latest headache for The Block
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCBD Fertile feral cats the latest headache for The Block Fiona Byrne Updated October 12, 2026 — 8:45am ,first published 5:33pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Renovations rarely go exactly to plan, so spare a thought for The Block, which is facing a potential kitten crisis as it prepares to make over three buildings at a former psychiatric hospital site in Sunbury. While Sunbury locals question the seemingly bargain $1.1 million price the production picked the properties in the former Caloola mental health and training precinct up for from the Victorian government, Animal Justice Party MP Georgie Purcell has raised an unexpected further concern for The Block to deal with – the welfare of a colony of fertile feral cats that inhabit the buildings 38 kilometres north-west of Melbourne’s inner-city grid. Victorian Animal Justice MP Georgie Purcell. Purcell has called on the show’s host, Scott Cam, and Nine, the owner of this masthead, to meet with her and cat conscious volunteers in the Sunbury area to negotiate a rehoming of the cluster of felines and their offspring. “Without intervention, this colony of unowned cats and kittens will come under serious threat when production crews start rolling in,” Purcell told CBD.



“There are a dedicated and amazing group of people who have been tending to these cats and stand ready, willing and able to capture, desex and rehome these animals – but they can’t do it alone. “While The Block isn’t responsible for causing this problem, they can be part of the solution and this is a chance for them to show some goodwill to the community, respect for animals rather than just profiting off development.” Three buildings from the former Sunbury psychiatric hospital will be turned into houses in next year’s season of The Block. Alamy Stock Photo Purcell said she had written to Nine, which owns the buildings through a company called MicJoy Pty Ltd, and funds and broadcasts the show, and had received a reply acknowledging her concerns. CBD also contacted Nine and we were told the network was aware of the cats.



“[We] are assessing the situation prior to their safe removal and construction commencing. We intend to keep all relevant stakeholders engaged throughout this process,” a spokesperson said. Meanwhile, someone purred to CBD over the weekend that while the cats were in the area they may not actually be living in the buildings bought by The Block. The twists keep coming! Now, there have been various dramas on The Block over the years, from permits to weather to bickering contestants and the occasional cranky nearby resident, but a brewing cat-astrophe? That is a first. Greg Norman takes swing at Qantas Australian golf legend Greg Norman has taken a very public swing at Qantas, calling it the “never on-time” airline and describing it as outdated and unreliable.



Norman, who was a high-profile celebrity ambassador for Qantas for decades, teed off at the airline’s management on Sunday, challenging them to get the service back up to his expected standard, adding the hashtag #alottodo to make his point. Australian golfing great Greg Norman has teed off at Qantas after his flight was delayed. Getty Images He also questioned whether profit had been put above “customer caring, reputation and service” and said it used to be one of the world’s top three airlines but “alas no more”. Known as the “Great white shark”, Norman took a fair bite out of Qantas, blasting it on his 244,000-strong Instagram account and saying he was now looking for another airline to travel with. Among other things, a lack of Wi-Fi on the long haul seems to have been part of what riled him up. US-based Norman recently attended the NRL grand final in Sydney and was travelling from Sydney to Dallas on a Qantas A380 at the weekend. A delay in leaving Sydney appears to have been the trigger for his epic spray.



“I have always tried to support my national airline @Qantas. Sadly, their reputation of the ‘never on-time’ airline (or the ones I am on – this time Syd-Dallas circa 3 hrs late departing) + an hour to get one bag in Dallas now has me looking elsewhere,” Norman fumed online. “Maybe @emirates longer but reliable, Wi-Fi, comfort caring. “Too bad, as @Qantas was once one of the top 3 in the world for a great travel experience. “Alas no more #whathappened Profit before customer caring, reputation and service!? Norman (left) was among the guests of the NRL, along with US ambassador David Brat (pink tie) and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese (foreground), at the 2026 NRL grand final.



“And not to have Wi-Fi in this day and age with the cost/ticket – #insane #dated. Ground staff excellent – Qantas Admin get to work and bring back the pride in – ‘The Spirit of Australia’ and be a world leader in your industry again!! #alottodo”. Not surprisingly, Qantas was well aware of Norman’s dummy spit when CBD called on Sunday morning. “Unfortunately, our flight from Sydney to Dallas Fort Worth on Saturday was delayed departing Sydney while our engineers fixed a fuelling issue,” a Qantas spokesperson told us, with no mention of Norman’s other gripes. No doubt someone will let Norman know Wi-Fi is in the process of being rolled out on Qantas’ A380 fleet, and is available on its 787s and A330 planes. But it might be too little too late, as it sounds like Norman will have swapped his boarding pass allegiances before that rollout is complete.



Brand-new look for Wood’s Brighton East gym There are more changes for former Bachelor star Sam Wood’s fitness empire – the huge and distinctive branding for his Brighton East gym, The Woodshed, has been taken down. Wood has long run The Woodshed and while his name remains on the venue’s website, the name The Woodshed disappeared from the outside of the two-storey building that houses the business on the Nepean Highway, sometime on Saturday. Sam Wood is facing domestic violence-related charges. The branding has for years made the gym hard to miss as you travel along the busy road.



Whether it is a temporary removal or a signal further change is coming is unclear. The Woodshed did not return our call on Sunday. Related Article Investigations ‘Imagine if I stuffed this up’: Sam Wood had the world, now it’s crashing down around him Founder Wood’s presence on the gym’s website seems to have been dialled back a bit. His name, however, is still contained in the Our Story tab, where it reads in part: “The Woodshed is proud to be known as Melbourne’s best training facility owned and operated by Australia’s leading Personal Trainer & Fitness Expert, Sam Wood.” The blurb ends: “We can’t wait to see you soon. Sam and the Woodshed Team.” Wood, however, is not seeing many people at the moment, given he is still in custody in Brisbane after being charged with domestic violence-related offences in Noosa this month.



Wood was denied bail by a Queensland magistrate on Thursday, as the court heard Snezana Wood, the wife of the former reality TV star, told police she feared he would kill her during an argument at an apartment in the popular holiday destination on October 3. Sam Wood’s lawyer Mathew Cuskelly said the circumstances may entitle his client to a self-defence argument, and indicated, after the hearing, the legal team would appeal the bail decision in the Supreme Court. World.title: Powderfinger reveal dates for national comeback tour
World.content:
Updated CultureMusicAustralian music Powderfinger reveal dates for national comeback tour Kayla Olaya and William Davis October 12, 2026 — 7:28am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Australian rock band Powderfinger have confirmed their national tour dates just days after announcing their reunion – and 16 years after breaking up. The 18-stadium show tour includes dates in Sydney, Melbourne, Cairns, Perth, and Adelaide and kicks off in the band’s hometown, Brisbane. Australian rock band Powderfinger have confirmed their national tour dates. Giulia Giannini McGauran Described on the band’s website as a “travelling rock’n’roll circus”, Powderfinger said the shows would be “part festival, part spectacle and set to be filled with the communal joy of thousands of fans, gathering offline to experience the music they love, together”. “We are absolutely ecstatic to be coming together to play again,” the band said in a statement posted to a new website on Monday morning. “Over the years there have been tons of suggestions for us to go back on the road but, until now, it never felt quite right or lined up for all of us.”



The band will curate an all-Australian line-up of support acts – with different artists joining in each city – and the tour is partnering with homeless charity Mission Australia. The tour dates are: Friday September 3 – Brisbane Showgrounds, Brisbane

Saturday September 4 – Brisbane Showgrounds, Brisbane

Friday September 10 – Brisbane Showgrounds, Brisbane

Saturday September 11 – Brisbane Showgrounds, Brisbane

Friday September 17 – Cazalys Stadium, Cairns

Saturday September 18 – Cazalys Stadium, Cairns

Friday September 24 – Wellington Square, Perth

Saturday September 25 – Wellington Square, Perth

Friday October 1 – The Domain, Sydney

Saturday October 2 – The Domain, Sydney

Friday October 8 – The Domain, Sydney

Saturday October 9 – The Domain, Sydney

Friday October 15 – Ellis Park, Adelaide

Saturday October 16 – Ellis Park, Adelaide

Friday October 22 – Melbourne Park Oval, Melbourne

Saturday October 23 – Melbourne Park Oval, Melbourne

Friday October 29 – Melbourne Park Oval, Melbourne

Saturday October 30 – Melbourne Park Oval, Melbourne Powderfinger tickets will go on presale on October 14 on Ticketmaster. Public sale will begin October 19, and all cities’ sale times are subject to their time zones. On Friday, the band uploaded videos to various social media platforms to confirm their reunion and announce a national tour after much speculation. “Hello, everyone. We’re Powderfinger, and we’ve got a little announcement to make for you today,” guitarist and vocalist Bernard “Bernie” Fanning said in the YouTube video.



“We always said that if we were going to get back together to do some shows, that you guys would be the first to know. And so now you’re the first to know. We’re going to do some shows all around Australia from September next year.” In the days leading up to the announcement, displays in Brisbane, Melbourne and Sydney featured sprawling letters, symbols and numbers connected to an Instagram account called The Return of the Electric Horsemen. Fans speculated it referenced Powderfinger’s song (Return of) The Electric Horseman from their 1996 album Double Allergic. Later, the band’s official Instagram posted the same image. Powderfinger. The band last performed at an impromptu reunion during Splendour in the Grass in 2017.



Fans perched above the Amphitheatre leapt to their feet and screamed with approval as Fanning’s former bandmates – Darren “Darius” Middleton, Ian “Hoggy” Haug and John “JC” Collins – readied their instruments. Drummer Jonathon “Cogsy” Coghill was the only absent member. Related Article Opinion

Australian music These days turned out nothing like I’d planned. Powderfinger just made sure of it Chris Paine National Content Director In the note to fans on their website, Powderfinger said support from both new and long-term fans had prompted the new tour. “It feels right to bring all of these people – including our kids who were too young to see us play – together for a special run of shows around the country next year,” the statement said. “People often tell us that our music is connected to their most treasured and joyous memories. We hope to spread a little more of that joy when we make our way around the country with some of Australia’s best established and upcoming talent, and to make some new memories for us all.“



The Queensland government took credit on Monday morning for securing back-to-back shows in the regional centre of Cairns, describing the concerts as a win for local businesses. “Powderfinger are Queensland legends, a Queensland story, so it’s only fitting that Queensland has secured this major coup,” Premier David Crisafulli said. “We went after this because we knew how much this would mean to Queenslanders, especially those in regional areas … Queensland has a plan to become the events capital of the country.” The state has repeatedly missed out on major touring acts, including Oasis, Taylor Swift and Coldplay.



Powderfinger formed in Brisbane in 1989 after Haug, an aspiring rock star who had played in pubs illegally as a teenager, created the band with two other high school friends, including Collins. Not long after, the five-piece as we know them today formed under a name inspired by a Neil Young song. In 1992, the band recorded their self-titled debut EP Powderfinger, also called The Blue. A second EP, Transfusion soon followed and in 1994 released debut album Parable for Wooden Ears. However, their 1996 release Double Allergic made them stars and they were soon touring worldwide, topping Triple J and ARIA charts, as well as booking big festival slots, including all dates for the Big Day Out. In total, Powderfinger have released seven studio albums, including anthems such as My Happiness, These Days, Sunsets, On My Mind, Burn Your Name and Pick You Up. World.title: Australia news LIVE: Greens to push for changes as Digital Duty of Care to be introduced to parliament this week; Frydenberg hints at political comeback, says Liberals ‘need to do better’

Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson says Australia should not be promoting violence, but will have trouble blocking the livestreaming of a US execution from being streamed in Australia.

“My basic principle is we shouldn’t be promoting that sort of violence, and so my fundamental view is yes, I think it’s enormously problematic to tolerate this type of behaviour,” he told ABC Radio National earlier when asked whether the government should block it.

“But the challenge is going to be how do you do that in a way that doesn’t amount to a censorship ban on the internet? How are you going to do that without creating the artifice to be able to block content on the internet and create an online portal of censorship?”

The execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring dozens more in a shooting at the Fort Hood military base in 2009, will be the first by military firing squad since World War II. The execution was approved by US President Donald Trump last week on the recommendation of Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth who originally said it would be a public event.

World.title: Woman stuck in Cook Islands for three years after NZ declines transit visa
World.content:
A foreign national has been stranded in the Cook Islands for three years. Despite assistance from Cook Islands Immigration, neither New Zealand nor Australia has approved a transit visa for her return home.

The 49-year-old arrived in the Cook Islands on 8 November 2023, and has been unable to leave since then. She also does not possess a visa to stay in the country. Neither Australia nor New Zealand has approved her transit, for which she does not even require leaving the Airport.

Cook Islands principal immigration officer Chere Arthur wrote to Immigration New Zealand on 11 April 2025, offering assistance by having someone escort the South Asian national to Auckland Airport until she boarded her connecting flight to Singapore.

Nothing has eventuated from Immigration New Zealand (INZ).

Responding to queries from Cook Islands News, Arthur said in an email that the Cook Islands government understands there is public interest in this matter.

"The individual remains in the Cook Islands not because options for departure have not been explored, but because of difficulties obtaining the transit visas needed to travel through other countries on the way to her final destination," Arthur said.

"Transit visas are issued by the countries a person needs to pass through during their journey. Decisions about these visas are made by those countries and are outside the control of the Cook Islands government.

"While the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Immigration has worked to identify possible travel arrangements, any departure depends on the approval of the necessary transit and travel documents by the relevant authorities.

"The government continues to manage the matter in accordance with the law and, to protect the individual's privacy, will not comment further on the details of the case."

INZ said it would comment on the matter when a privacy waiver is provided to them authorising this newspaper to seek responses on the foreign national's behalf.

A waiver or a consent was provided to INZ on Friday; however, because of time differences, no reply has been forthcoming yet.

New Zealand High Commissioner to the Cook Islands Catherine Graham said she had contacted Wellington.

"I've contacted the relevant team in Wellington for a response and will come back to you as soon as I can. As it is the weekend, I don't imagine I'll get a response until our Sunday at the earliest," she told Cook Islands News.

Questions sent to the Australian High Commission remain unanswered.

The foreign national left her country after her husband was killed. She worked in Hong Kong for almost a year before being granted a work visa in New Zealand in March 2023. Whilst working, she applied for an asylum visa.

The woman claimed that while her visa was being processed, she was told by the lawyer helping her out that she needed to leave New Zealand and return later.

World.title: Second intimate video controversy hits Fiji  government
World.content:
The Fijian government has found itself caught up in another scandal after an explicit video involving one of its cabinet ministers ended up in the public domain on the eve of Fiji Day.

According to local media reports over the weekend, the one-minute clip appeared on a prominent male minister's Facebook profile on Friday night before it was taken down.

"The Minister concerned has not made any comments since yesterday, and has also not said whether his account was hacked or whether it was accidentally put up," a report on fijivillage.com on Saturday said.

"He has also not confirmed if the Online Safety Commission has been alerted as the video is now being circulated," it reported.

This is the second time an intimate recording of a Fiji government minister has surfaced online under Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka's administration.

An intimate video involving a female cabinet minister was leaked online and went viral on Christmas Eve in 2024, with the minister stating the private recording was originally intended for her husband.

The minister was suspended by Rabuka and removed as a cabinet minister in early 2025, though returned to a new portfolio later.

The latest video scandal has dominated Fijian social media over the weekend.

In its frontpage story on Monday, the Fiji Sun reported that the prime minister is challenging anyone making allegations against the minister concerned to come forward with evidence and testify.

"I want someone ready to testify against my minister so I can give him the opportunity to defend himself," Rabuka was quoted as saying by the newspaper.

World.title: Labour plans to cut school uniform costs and allow 'affordable, generic' options
World.content:
Labour wants to cut back-to-school costs for families by making school uniforms cheaper and allow for "affordable, generic" alternatives to be used as well.

Labour Leader Chris Hipkins says getting kids ready for school "shouldn't mean starting the term with another big bill."

"Families are already stretched, and school costs can push household budgets to the limit."

Hipkins said parents deserve a "fair go", and Labour would cut the cost of school uniforms, bring back healthy school lunches and work towards restoring rural school buses, "taking pressure off family budgets."

"Cost should never be a barrier to a good education. We're focused on making life more affordable for families," Hipkins said.

He explained that school uniforms would be made cheaper by limiting the number of compulsory branded items schools can require and allowing affordable, generic alternatives that meet uniform requirements.

Under Labour, schools would be required to:

Limit the number of compulsory branded uniform items families must buy.

Allow affordable, non-branded alternatives that meet school uniform requirements.

Take affordability into account when setting uniform policies.

Track and publish uniform costs so progress towards making uniforms cheaper can be measured.

Labour education spokesperson Ginny Andersen said "schools can maintain their identity without forcing parents to pay a premium for a logo."

Labour education spokesperson Ginny Andersen. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

"If a plain navy polo does the job, parents shouldn't have to pay more for the branded version."

Andersen said cheaper uniforms were just one part of Labour's plan.

The party would also bring back locally made school lunches from Term 1 2028 and restore the 43 rural school bus routes National cancelled, "where possible." It would work with communities where routes can no longer be reinstated, Andersen added.

"That means lower costs for families, reliable transport for rural kids and healthy lunches that help children learn," she said.

World.title: 'Imminent threat' of drought in Niue, yellow alert declared
World.content:
Niue is under a yellow alert for an imminent threat of drought.

Niue's disaster management ffice says wildfires have already happened in several areas - Tualihega, Kavata, Paluki, Tumau-Alofi, Liku and Hakupu.

The government said water infrastructure and plantations have been damaged.

"The decision follows a series of fire incidents that have resulted in damage to critical water infrastructure and plantations, while also placing homes, property, and essential services at significant risk."

The National Disaster Council has assessed that the threat has moved beyond a potential hazard and now requires immediate protective action, including a total burn ban.

It said there was an "extremely high" fire risk in Niue.

Meanwhile, the New Zealand Defence Force (NZDF) has provided a 4WD firefighting truck and equipment.

The C-130 aircraft also brought a Fire and Emergency New Zealand (FENZ) team, personal protective clothing, and drone mapping equipment with thermal imaging capability.

FENZ national commander Megan Stiffler said the New Zealand contingent will provide training and technical advice to Niue firefighting staff to help them manage wildfire risks.

The NZ High Commission in Niue said the FENZ team would provide specialist technical advice, operational planning, and logistical support to help manage ongoing wildfire risks, and will also support recovery efforts and strengthen Niue's future fire management capability and resilience.

"This work is especially important as El Niño forecasts indicate that dry conditions in Niue will likely persist in the coming months, with the risk of bushfires remaining elevated."

El Niño is underway in the Pacific, bringing dry conditions to several areas.

The Tonga Meteorological Service has declared drought across all major islands that make up the kingdom, including Tongatapu, Niuatoputapu, Ha'apai and 'Eua.

World.title: Man charged with murder over Christchurch double killing appears in court
World.content:
A man has appeared in court charged with murdering two people in the Christchurch suburb of Phillipstown.

Two other people were badly hurt at the property in Olliviers Road.

Rodney Stewart Smith, 58, is facing two charges of murder, one of attempted murder and another of grievous bodily harm following the deaths early on Saturday morning.

He is accused of murdering Glen Allan Tukaki and Nigel John Robinson, attempting to murder James Alan Dell and wounding Shantay Marie McQuade with intent to cause grievous bodily harm.

Police were called to an address on Olliviers Road last week. Louis Dunham/RNZ

He is also charged with intentionally damaging a car.
